Following a micropolitical analysis of ‘the secret’ and secrecy in terms of flows of power and resistance, the paper applies Deleuze and Guattari’s argument that the prime objective of a capitalist state is to assure free flows of matter, labour and money that enable capital accumulation and economic growth. It uses Deleuze’s ethological ontology and methodology to analyse micropolitically undercover infiltrations of domestic anti-capitalist organisations and clandestine overseas interventions. The paper concludes that the secret state contributes to an architecture of control that sustains the material flows upon which capitalism depends.
10.1177/07255136261458834.title: Capitalism and state secrecy: A micropolitics of material flows, covert operations and control

10.1177/07255136261458836.abstract: The article develops the concept of algorithmic publicity to theorize the pre-discursive structuring of visibility in digital environments. It argues that algorithmic infrastructures shape the conditions under which content becomes publicly accessible, relocating the dynamics of communicative rationality and systemic coordination to the infrastructural level. Drawing on Jürgen Habermas, the argument situates these developments within the trajectory of modernity as a reconfiguration rather than a rupture. Existing approaches, including communicative capitalism, platform society and surveillance capitalism, remain focused on processes within visibility, leaving its underlying conditions insufficiently theorized. Algorithmic publicity addresses this gap by conceptualizing visibility as a regime produced by predictive systems that operate prior to communication. This transformation extends the systemic media of money and power into the formation of visibility. The ‘Fediverse’ is introduced as a conceptual test case, illustrating the contingency and contestability of these infrastructural arrangements.
10.1177/07255136261458836.title: Algorithmic publicity: Rethinking the conditions of visibility in the public sphere

10.1177/07255136261458837.abstract: Employing the tools of biographical sociology, this paper analyses the life narratives of two East European intellectuals: Hungarian-born Ágnes Heller and Polish-born Andrzej Walicki. Both scholars, whose trajectories display striking parallels, emigrated first to Australia and then to the United States, returning only in old age to their countries of origin. Their academic paths are interpreted through the concept of the ‘deep story’, understood as the emotional core of a worldview. Although Heller and Walicki left for different reasons, both were academic sojourners – individuals who longed for their homelands, never fully integrated into the university cultures of the receiving countries, and grappled with cultural contact and political entanglements beyond academia. This paper contributes to intellectual history by examining homegrown academic success, expulsion, attempts at ‘homemaking’ abroad, and eventual return, while also offering insight into humanities careers that remain deeply rooted in national cultures and embedded within broader intellectual traditions.
10.1177/07255136261458837.title: East European public intellectuals as academic sojourners: Analysing the deep stories in the life narratives of Ágnes Heller and Andrzej Walicki

10.1177/07255136261459467.abstract: In this article we arrest the concept of ‘power-seeking’ away from apocalyptic discourses about AI's future risks to humanity. Following Latour, we suggest that while non-human actors may ‘authorize, allow, afford, encourage…[etc.]’, they can also seek power . We explain how power-seeking as a potential non-human ‘program of action’– specifically, the pursuit of increasing abilities, or authority or control over other actors – facilitates analysis of networks that enable or curb the development of technologies founded on future imaginaries. To illustrate the potential utility of power-seeking as an agency of non-human actors in the new materialist theoretical repertoire, we apply it to AI large language models, focusing on the banal reality of today's chatbots. Overall, we advance ‘power-seeking’ as a conceptual tool to analyse human–non-human dynamics, power and agency, and how associations produce outcomes that are more or less harmful or beneficial to collectives.
10.1177/07255136261459467.title: From apocalyptic dystopia to banal reality: A new materialist account of power-seeking, AI and chatbots

10.1177/07255136261459469.abstract: Governance on the European periphery is frequently diagnosed through the lens of ‘incapacity’ or ‘failed modernization.’ Yet, such diagnostics overlook how dysfunction itself operates as a specific technology of power. This article advances a critical theory of the state by analysing what I term projectocracy. This regime governs not through the production of rational order, but through the strategic management of productive failure. Drawing on ethnographic fieldwork in post-socialist Romania, I analyse how the subjects of this regime − far from being passive victims − actively curate the state's fictions. My main argument is that these citizens perform the immaterial labour necessary to sustain the bureaucratic apparatus while pursuing their own survival in the shadows. Ultimately, I posit that the state survives not by eliminating its informal shadow, but by becoming structurally dependent upon the very parallel worlds it pretends not to see.
10.1177/07255136261459469.title: The ungovernable governed: Projectocracy and the complicit state

10.1177/07255136261459470.abstract: This article examines the failure of recent political uprisings in post-revolutionary Iran through the framework of Peripheral Capitalist Realism (PCR), extending Mark Fisher's notion of ideological foreclosure. PCR describes a political-affective condition produced by the fusion of authoritarian governance, predatory accumulation, patrimonialism, and neoliberal rationality in a peripheral theocracy. Drawing on survey data from 332 educated, urban middle-class respondents and critical theory, the study argues that beyond state repression, the internalization of neoliberal values and absence of viable alternatives generate resignation and affective withdrawal. Integrating Fisher's ideas of “reflexive impotence” and “privatization of stress” with Lauren Berlant's “cruel optimism” and Marxist analyses of peripheral capitalism, the paper shows how Iranian society embodies a distinctive capitalist realism shaped by its unique blend of Islamic theocracy and predatory economics. Empirical findings reveal precarious labor, psychological distress, and a pervasive desire to emigrate, indicating a socio-political atmosphere where systemic transformation appears increasingly unimaginable.
10.1177/07255136261459470.title: Peripheral capitalist realism: Theorizing the affective foreclosure of futurity in Iran

10.1177/07255136261459471.abstract: Against broader readings that extend reification across different social spheres, this article argues that the concept gains analytical precision when anchored in the economic fabric of society. It understands reification as arising from capitalist societalisation mediated by the commodity form. The concept designates a double form of power: first, the impersonal and abstract power generated by commodity-mediated relations; and second, the ideological power through which this historically specific order appears natural and unchangeable, fostering economic fatalism. The article also distinguishes reification from capitalist rationalisation, showing how fragmented rational calculation both presupposes and reproduces an irrational social totality. It further highlights the non-essentialist account of subjectivity on which the theory relies and clarifies the relation between reification and capitalist alienation. In doing so, it outlines a more precise framework for historicising reification and analysing its relation to socio-economic and political phenomena in contemporary capitalism.
10.1177/07255136261459471.title: Reification re-specified: The power of commodity-mediated societalisation

10.1177/07255136261461708.title: Book Review: Revolutions: A New History by Donald Sassoon SassoonDonald, Revolutions: A New History (Verso, London, 2025); 426 pp. £30; US $39.95; ISBN: 1804299920

10.1177/07255136261464658.abstract: Jeffrey Alexander presented culture as acting autonomously in shaping outcomes in the civil sphere, by way of narratives, symbolic binaries and social performances. Using Viviana Zelizer and her academic progeny as his touchstone, Alexander analysed from above how cultural structure shaped economic action and the workings of markets, entering the territory of economic sociology and of economics where the dynamics of dramaturgical performances remained limited to Erving Goffman, religious-like performances to Randall Collins. With Zelizer, he was aligned, though his analysis worked from the top down, while her relational work discerned the cultural structure from the bottom up. For the economists and for traditional economic sociologists, culture had trespassed into territory they controlled. This article reviews how cultural sociology boldly entered the marketplace.
10.1177/07255136261464658.title: Trespassing into economic life: Alexander and Zelizer, Alexander and me

10.1177/07255136261464660.abstract: For nearly half a century Jeffrey C. Alexander has devoted himself to the sociological vocation − first as a general (‘grand’) theorist, and then as the iconic leader of a set of global research programmes − a life lived for sociology. In ‘Part 1’ of this two-part article, we make the case for Alexander's canonization as a classical theorist. We do so by reconstructing and periodizing his life and intellectual development, narrating his transformation from Jeff to ‘Jeffrey C. Alexander.’ We do this at the level of what Parsons's termed personality : that is, we situate Alexander's oeuvre in the quality of his person, his wants and needs, his frustrations and anxieties, and the development of the self.
10.1177/07255136261464660.title: Reading Jeffrey C. Alexander, Part I: The case for canonization

10.1177/07255136261464662.abstract: In this article, I respond to the overview and exegesis of Alexander's sociology provided by Villegas and Watts. I explore their case for the theorist's ‘canonization’ and outline what they see as the major ‘commitments’ of his social theory. As someone who self-defines as a cultural sociologist, I am particularly interested in what the authors term the ‘multidimensionality’ and ‘postpositivism’ of Alexander's thought. However, I also note Villegas and Watts identify a possible shortcoming: namely, whether Alexander's cultural sociology pays sufficient attention to the materiality of social life. What I call ‘Cultural Sociology 2.0’ has linked meaning to materiality more explicitly; and rather than positing culture as an ‘independent’ or ‘dependent’ variable has gravitated towards nonlinear models of culture. I conclude by asking whether cultural sociology is a style of analysis; and suggest both preserving the ‘black boxes’ of meaning and being attentive to things at the ‘edges’ of comprehension.
10.1177/07255136261464662.title: Cultural sociology and the ‘black box’ of meaning: Responding to Villegas and Watts's ‘Reading Jeffrey C. Alexander’

10.1177/07255136261464663.abstract: In ‘Part II’ of this two-part article, we provide a general schematic with which to introduce the Alexanderian vision of sociology. This vision comprises the following five commitments: (a) a commitment to structural voluntarism and the moral dimension of human action; (b) a commitment to multidimensionality; (c) a commitment to the centrality of meaning in social life, and thus to culture's autonomy; (d) a commitment to a postpositivist conception of social science; and (e) a commitment to democracy as a utopian ideal. In addition to elaborating this vision, we also explore its theoretical tensions and strains, and the way these serve as a fecund source of generative thought and theoretical development − giving rise to new problems, as well as new attempts at resolution.
10.1177/07255136261464663.title: Reading Jeffrey C. Alexander, Part II: The theoretical core (and its tensions)

10.1177/07255136261464665.abstract: This article reflects on my intellectual journey into cultural sociology and the work of Jeffrey C. Alexander. Beginning with an ethnographic study of theatre for young audiences, I describe how encounters with the Strong Program in Cultural Sociology opened new analytical possibilities for understanding how meaning emerges in the stage−audience encounter. From this point, the value of an ethnographic perspective on civil sphere theory, which I call civil sphere ethnography, helps to bring the civil sphere into view within everyday situations, interactions and emotional dynamics. The article provides an example of how processes of civil repair can occur in a local educational setting within contemporary Swedish society, characterized by increasing diversity and segregation. By connecting Alexander with Paulo Freire, I outline a pedagogical approach I call the critical pedagogy of multicultural incorporation, highlighting its potential to foster recognition, reduce shame, enhance a sense of belonging and, hopefully, broaden civil inclusion.
10.1177/07255136261464665.title: A journey into cultural sociology

10.1177/07255136261464668.abstract: This comment on Villegas and Watt's reflective overview of Jeffrey Alexander's scholarly contributions, addresses canonization, the value of sociological tensions and neglected empirical components of his work.
10.1177/07255136261464668.title: Tensions and insights: More on ‘Reading Jeffrey C. Alexander’

10.1177/07255136261464671.abstract: What is the basis of canonization for social theorists? An accounting of the career of the prominent American sociologist Jeffrey Alexanders points to the basis of this reputational claim and its limitations. Alexander is one of the most widely respected theorists of the past half-century but viewing his broad interests in politics and civil society and his promotion of the Strong Program in cultural sociology provides a justification for his widely-acclaimed importance and the basis for the paired articles to which this squib is a response.
10.1177/07255136261464671.title: Saint Jeff

10.1177/07255136261464674.abstract: The article expands upon Villegas and Watts’ call for Jeffrey C. Alexander's work to be recognised as part of a renewed sociological canon by exploring the contemporary political complexity of establishing a neoclassical paradigm generally and the inclusion of Alexander specifically. Drawing on the sociology of intellectual movements, it is argued that elevating the status of Alexander would afford the discipline an important way to come to terms with recent shifts in democracy, nationalism and global power.
10.1177/07255136261464674.title: The politics and promise of Alexanderian neoclassical sociology

10.1177/07255136261464675.abstract: What makes a body of work ‘canonical’? In his writings over the years Jeffrey C. Alexander offers some phenomenologically convincing answers, each suggesting that the power of canonical texts is simultaneously context-immanent and context-transcending. However, a critical theory of ‘the canon’ cannot confine itself to phenomenological description. A critical theory is necessary due to the social constitution of the meanings of canonical texts. This gives rise to an endemic risk of ideological biases and the danger that canonization will reproduce and reinforce dominant perceptions of intellectual value, excluding or marginalizing authors and works who do not fit well with these perceptions. Accordingly, theories cognizant of this risk must explain the context-transcending component of the normativity of canonical works in a non-reductive way. This is a challenge for critical sociology.
10.1177/07255136261464675.title: Criticizing ‘the canon:’ A challenge for cultural sociology

10.1177/07255136261464682.abstract: No contemporary social-theoretical thinker has been more attuned to matters of verbal representation, literary genres, and the dramatic force of words and imagery than Jeffrey C. Alexander. Taking its lead from Villegas and Watts’ appreciation of him, this paper offers a jeu d’esprit of intellectual appreciation that traverses the ancient and modern worlds. It considers various literary genres and tropes involved in the creation of appreciative biographical writing. Riffing on terms such as Alexanderian, Alexandrian, Alexandrine and Alexanderesque, it relates Jeffrey C. Alexander, as biographical persona, to his antique namesake, Alexander the Great. The Greatness of the modern person(a) is brought into high relief through comparison with his ancient counterpart. The paper follows in the parallel footsteps of Alexander the ancient and Alexander the modern, seeking to exhibit some of their own respective forms of audacity in daring to make such a comparison.
10.1177/07255136261464682.title: From Alexander the Great to Alexander's Greatness, and back again: An ancient/modern jeu d’esprit of intellectual appreciation

10.1177/07255136261467761.abstract: Richard Wagner's Bayreuth Festival is presented as a ‘goldmine’ case study for sociology. Durkheimian approaches to the body overwhelmingly draw on the Elementary Forms to emphasize its productive role. Bodily ritual, rhythm and regulation help us experience the solidary force of the sacred. Durkheim's essay on The Duality of Human Nature adds complexity to this picture. Here Durkheim sees the body as blocking access to higher forms of social thought, as being egoistic rather than solidaristic, and as preventing focused attention on civilizational projects. This paper presents a new set of Durkheimian questions. It directs sociological inquiry to research the body not only as a resource but also as a barrier to transcendence. Furthermore, this paper takes up the challenge with reference to the experiences of opera fans at Bayreuth. A broader Durkheimian agenda would offer a more capacious sociology of the body and the sacred.
10.1177/07255136261467761.title: Durkheim, the body and the sacred: The neglected lesson of Homo duplex illustrated by the Wagner Bayreuth Festival

10.1177/07255136261467762.abstract: Angela Davis argues that Billie Holiday's music retains an “undiminished appeal” across generations because it can simultaneously “confirm and subvert racist and sexist representations of women” in romantic love. In this article, Davis's argument is extended through an examination of Holiday's narratives about and lived experience with a different kind of love: friendship. Friendship is detailed first as an ideal in the aesthetic partnership Holiday shared with tenor saxophonist Lester Young. Then, friendship's constraints are considered through Holiday's narratives about connections she made in childhood and with Benny Goodman, Artie Shaw, and Orson Welles. Where Holiday's love songs highlight the confines of sexism and racism, her reflections on friendship include classism and sexuality, and thereby provide insight into the ways intersectionality works to squeeze the potential for freedom and shared growth by coalescing around the identities that are either had by, or presumed of, those who share the friendship.
10.1177/07255136261467762.title: Billie Holiday on the constraints of friendship and a lived ideal

10.1177/07255136261467763.abstract: This article reimagines Postcolonial Security Studies (PSS) through the allegory of ancestors. It examines two generations of responses to coloniality in Security Studies – Third World Security Studies and Decolonial Security Studies – highlighting their fundamental contribution to the formation and evolution of PSS, while noting their partial disconnection from the ideas and traditions of the South. These often-ignored contributions could offer a deeper understanding of violence, state formation and liberation rooted in anti-colonial struggles. Rather than finding an epistemic rupture, the article argues for recovering liberation entities from formal and informal referents that carry memory and meaning. The examples of Brazil's Tambor de Sopapo and South Africa's Makhanda demonstrate how marginalised legacies might reorient the field. The article advances a people-centred PSS grounded in historical and community-based perspectives. This approach challenges Eurocentric frameworks and affirms the significance of knowledges and knowings of the South in theorising Security.
10.1177/07255136261467763.title: Never forget your ancestors: Reimagining postcolonial security studies

10.1177/07255136261467764.title: The eternal return: Bourdieu and reflexivity A review essay of: Bourdieu P (2025) Return to Reflexivity. Edited by Bourdieu J and Heilbron J, translated by Collier P. Cambridge: Polity Press.

10.1177/07255136261467765.abstract: This article examines dystopian literature as a critical counterpart to sociology, emphasizing its role in social self-description. The author introduces the concept of the sublimation of the negative, inspired by Niklas Luhmann, to explain how dystopias transform the negative side of self-descriptive social codes into tools for critical thought. The re-introduction of the distinction of good/evil allows dystopia to unmask the latent ‘social evil’ hidden within the utopias of efficiency promoted by other systems such as politics, science, or the economy, which are often blind to their own human costs. Unlike sociology, which often avoids speculative and future-oriented inquiries, dystopias embrace imaginative alternatives, addressing epistemic gaps such as de-futurization and the marginalization of subjective experience. Through analyses of works such as Gabriel de Tarde's The Underground Man , Edward Morgan Forster's The Machine Stops and Janusz A. Zajdel's Limes inferior , the article demonstrates dystopia's ability to transcend sociological explanatory schemes.
10.1177/07255136261467765.title: Dystopia and the limits of sociological thought: A critical exploration

10.1177/07255136261467766.abstract: This article examines how sustainability is rendered publicly legitimate in the current phase of green capitalism. Rather than treating environmental, social, and governance (ESG) as mere ideology or Solarpunk as external critique, it approaches both as modalities of public testing within a shared moral field. Drawing on Boltanski and Thévenot's sociology of justification, it argues that ecological legitimacy today is structured by a dominant normative test embedded in ESG discourse and a subordinate yet consequential sensible test, in which sustainability must also appear credible within shared perceptual horizons. To conceptualize this second dimension, the article introduces the notion of épreuve de sensibilité : a public test of rightness operating on the affective and aesthetic plane. Through a comparative analysis of European ESG regulatory texts (2019–2025) and a multilingual corpus of Solarpunk narratives (2012–2024), it shows how ecological morality is stabilized as procedural coherence in governance and staged as perceptual consonance in cultural imaginaries
10.1177/07255136261467766.title: Captured by the sun? Solarpunk, environmental, social, and governance criteria, and the pragmatics of green justification

10.1177/07255136261470444.abstract: This review essay critically engages Andrew Hartman's Karl Marx in America , a reception history of three different classes of readings of Marx's writings in the United States. The essay's main contention is that Hartman's text, however unintentionally, seems to deviate from and thus challenges the anti-foundational principles that orient the genre of reception history. For, echoing Shakespeare's, Hegel's, and Marx's uses of the metaphor of the “Old Mole,” Hartman's own commitment to a labor-oriented version of “Marx”—from the three he charts in his topography of the Marx–America dialectic—works its way through Karl Marx in America , appearing at the end of text to subvert the groundless doctrines that guide reception histories.
10.1177/07255136261470444.title: “Well grubbed, old mole!”: On Karl Marx in America by Andrew Hartman, University of Chicago Press, 2025

10.1177/07255136261473942.abstract: This interview with the philosopher Raymond Geuss, Professor Emeritus of Philosophy at the University of Cambridge, explores the questions animating his 2026 book Tracks in Chaos: Philosophical Orientation and Political Reflection (Polity). The book's title invokes Heidegger's image of the Holzweg – forest tracks cut through labour that often lead nowhere – which Geuss develops into a figure for philosophy as a historically situated, constrained, and dependent activity rather than an autonomous system. Drawing on his formation in Heidegger, Marx, and Adorno, he defends a suspicion of ordinary language and everyday concepts, proposing a ‘binary vision’ for operating within social practices while seeing through them. He distinguishes three senses of authority, none of which philosophy can claim, and separates ‘moralising’ from moral judgement proper. The interview closes with his diagnosis of a disintegrating West, marked by concentrated wealth and power, financialisation, technological deskilling, and a pervasive loss of orientation.
10.1177/07255136261473942.title: Paths to nowhere: An interview with Raymond Geuss about Tracks in Chaos

10.1177/07255136261473945.title: Book Review: A Hopeful Political Imagination: Courage and Fantastic Critique in the Age of Meltdown by Oscar Guardiola-Rivera Guardiola-RiveraOscar. A Hopeful Political Imagination: Courage and Fantastic Critique in the Age of Meltdown. New York: Bloomsbury Academic, 2025. 280 pp. ISBN (hardback) 9781666974454.

10.1177/07255136261480121.abstract: This article undertakes a historical-critical investigation of the intertwining of critical theory and functionalism in steps. It takes Adorno's critique of functionalism in architecture as a point of departure to distinguish the specific sense in which ‘functionalism’ is defined and subsequently rejected. The following section scrutinizes how critical theory deploys functionalist explanation, consciously or unconsciously, as the operative dynamic of its social diagnosis. On this basis, the third section utilises previously articulated methodological distinctions to outline critical theory's attempts at a normative reconstruction of the category of ‘function’. Then the inquiry pivots to the debates within analytical Marxism to examine critical theory's over-reliance on ‘objective teleology’ within its social diagnosis. Finally, the paper returns to the primary texts of sociological functionalism to refute critical theory's stereotype that equates function with end, thereby recovering more sophisticated understandings of functionalism for sociological analysis.
10.1177/07255136261480121.title: ‘Functionalist prejudice’: Critical theory and teleology

10.1177/07255136261480126.abstract: With the precipitous decline of functionalism as a theoretical paradigm, sociologists have become increasingly skeptical of descriptive claims about the functions of social phenomena. Despite this, ongoing debates about the function term in biology and philosophy have led many to reconsider the utility of functionalist language. Contributing to these debates, this article examines the value of talk about societal level functions. Specifically, I examine whether contemporary theories of the function term allow us to make objective distinctions between the functions of an item for society and the effects it has on society. Assessing several prominent accounts, I show that current approaches to the function/effect distinction continue to leave us with conceptual problems when applied at the societal level. The analysis suggests that the function term offers few explanatory benefits, and that we are right to remain wary of present efforts to revitalize functionalist thought.
10.1177/07255136261480126.title: Functional analysis at the societal level: Are there any pathways forward?

10.1177/07255136261480129.abstract: This contribution explores power and solidarity in Merleau-Ponty's phenomenology, bringing together his reflections on the social world in Phenomenology of Perception with his appraisal of sociology and Marxism in Signs and Adventures of the Dialectic . I argue that Merleau-Ponty reconfigures power as the crystallization of social interest that connects individuals and groups despite the differences in their social and political membership. This paves the way for a reconsideration of solidarity as the power to institute a different sense of reality from the shared experience of work and oppression. I conclude with an illustration of the contingency of solidarity in connection with the social struggle that led to the Italian law 199/2016 against the exploitation of undocumented workers.
10.1177/07255136261480129.title: Power and solidarity in Merleau-Ponty's phenomenology

10.1177/07255136261480130.abstract: This article argues that democratic double standards are not episodes of normative inconsistency but a mutable political technology for the differential distribution of legitimacy. The concept names a historically changing ensemble of institutional apparatuses, justificatory rationalities and material infrastructures through which the threshold of democratic legitimacy is unevenly allocated while its political function persists. It is distinguished from organised hypocrisy, ideology and discourse by four features: a function/mechanism distinction, institutional materiality, genealogical temporality and colonial asymmetry. The argument unfolds through a theory-generating genealogy organised around the Chile–Brazil axis – a historically dense dyad that condenses the technology in unusually legible form. Three moments of mutation are reconstructed: anti-communist destabilisation in Chile, the regionalisation of repression through Operation Condor and the reorganisation of political antagonism in Brazil. Integrating governmentality and the coloniality of power, it approaches Latin America as a theoretical archive for theorising the unevenness of democratic universalism.
10.1177/07255136261480130.title: Democratic double standards as a mutable political technology: A historical genealogy from Latin America

10.1177/07255136261485212.abstract: Contemporary critical theory elevates social norms to the status of positive knowledge and proclaims a politics of normative rightness to realise positive freedom and material equality in capitalist society. By accepting the positivity of norms, it fetishises them and prevents their denunciation, which alone exposes them. Based on the critical theories of Marx and Adorno, the article examines social norms as norms of a historically specific social content. In this process, the freedom of form is exposed in its content as the ‘freedom to starve’ (Adorno). Critique of exploitation does not call for normative arguments to understand its normative deficiencies with a view to achieving improvements. To understand the social norms, one must think in and through them to grasp their secret in the freedom of labour, which is the freedom of needy individuals to secure wage income. The circumstance that their prospects depend on the profitability of their labour connects the (promise of) freedom with exploitation.
10.1177/07255136261485212.title: Normative values and social critique: On Adorno and Marx

10.1177/07255136261485214.abstract: Neal Harris's Critical Theory and the Critique of Alternative Societies represents a significant contribution to the revival of first-generation Frankfurt School critical theory and its application to the contemporary alternative societies movement. This review essay evaluates Harris's central argument – that experimental pluralism among alternative societies is undermined by insufficient critique and an actionist displacement of strategic thinking – by placing it in dialogue with the existing scholarship on real utopias, workers’ cooperatives, mutual aid and universal basic income. The essay affirms the explanatory power of Harris's Frankfurt School framework, particularly his deployment of reification, instrumental rationality and repressive desublimation, while raising critical questions about the scope of the analysis, the tension between negativity and praxis and the risk of reproducing a specifically Western, male-centred theoretical horizon. The review ultimately endorses Harris's call for a renewed synthesis of critique and activism as an urgent priority for critical social theory.
10.1177/07255136261485214.title: Critique at the crossroads: On Neal Harris's Critical Theory and the Critique of Alternative Societies A review essay of Neal Harris (2026), Critical Theory and the Critique of Alternative Societies: Co-operatives, Mutual Aid and Universal Basic Income, Manchester: Manchester University Press, 254 pp. ISBN 978 1 5261 7222 8.

10.1177/07255136261487198.abstract: This introductory article critiques dominant, teleological social science narratives that position organised violence as a declining historical phenomenon. Instead, it asserts the structural centrality of warfare as a primary catalyst for institutional, political and societal transformation across human history. The author examines the dynamic relationship between organised violence and systemic social change, demonstrating how large-scale conflicts continue to reshape contemporary social orders. Finally, the text analyses the distinct features of war and peace in the modern era and provides a comprehensive overview of the nine academic contributions that compose this special issue.
10.1177/07255136261487198.title: War and peace in the early 21st century: An introduction

10.1177/07255136261487199.abstract: Culturally specific collective memories often give rise to potent and emotional historical analogues, used to mobilize people and to understand new situations. This article examines such emotional analogues through the still dominant but highly selective Finnish collective memory of the Winter War, which shaped the Finnish public discourse of the War in Ukraine after 2022. The Winter War constitutes a central building block for Finnish national identity. The similarities between the Winter War and the War in Ukraine helped make the latter more relatable among the Finnish society. The emotions raised by the analogue helped with the mobilization of sympathy for the Ukrainian cause. Simultaneously, the piecemeal use of the Winter War analogue transposed mythical expectations from Finnish collective memory on Ukrainians in a manner that biased attempts to understand the ongoing war. By linking socially constructed collective war memories to emotional historical analogues, the article emphasizes the importance of cultural sociology of war.
10.1177/07255136261487199.title: Collective memories, emotional analogues and war: How the Winter War shaped the Finnish public understanding of the War in Ukraine

10.1177/07255136261487201.abstract: This article examines the disappearance of the liberal peace paradigm. I examine how peace itself ceases to exist by drawing on the case of Kibbutz Be’eri, long associated with Israel's peace camp and known for its close ties with residents of Gaza, in which dozens of residents were killed or taken hostage, and its response to the October 7 massacre. The Be’eri residents were confronted with a triple shock: (a) the sudden and unexpected massacre; (b) the profound break of trust and feelings of abandonment from the state; and (c) the failure of their core belief in the liberal peace paradigm. I argue that three interconnected features – Trump's version of peace that excludes peace; the state-led projects of narratives of resilience, bravery, and heroism; and the Be’eri residents’ public disclosure of pain – made (liberal) peace obsolete and ousted it from the political horizon.
10.1177/07255136261487201.title: Is peace becoming obsolete? The Kibbutz Be’eri file

10.1177/07255136261487203.abstract: This article examines how the embodied and material consequences of violent conflict shape long-term processes of post-war reconciliation and closure. Wars subject human bodies to death, disappearance, displacement, torture and other forms of extreme harm, producing effects that reverberate across generations. Yet, despite the central role of corporeality in conflict, limited attention has been paid to how bodily experiences, or the absence of bodies, inform efforts to repair and transform violence, including reconciliation initiatives. Focusing on the unresolved issue of missing persons, this article explores how the absence of bodies constrains or enables possibilities for reconciliation over extended periods. It does so through an analysis of the First World War's Western Front in Belgium and France, where around 700,000 soldiers remain without known graves. By tracing the century-long afterlives of these disappearances, the article highlights the enduring influence of corporeal loss on post-war social and political transformation.
10.1177/07255136261487203.title: Reconciliation without closure: The long-term legacies of disappearances after the First World War

10.1177/07255136261487204.abstract: The American military–industrial complex is currently undergoing a profound transformation, recasting the triangle of political, military and corporate power anatomised by C. Wright Mills. Anchored in federally directed scientific research and a shared elite commitment to the geopolitical primacy of the militarised national state, the Cold War historical formation of the military–industrial complex was bound by a ‘military metaphysics’ that posited war as the era's defining necessity. This order has progressively unravelled with the shifting locus of technological development to the commercial sector. Pivoting away from the procurement process dominated by the defence primes during the War on Terror, the Pentagon has for the last decade courted Silicon Valley's tech giants and venture-backed start-ups in the pursuit of decisive military advantage amidst intensifying geopolitical competition. While the triangle's institutional orders persist, their hierarchy is now being inverted. Through its growing infrastructural power, ideological assertiveness and colonisation of political and military elites, a tech-capital pole is increasingly setting the terms for the whole. A new technological metaphysics is ascendant, affirming technological supremacy as the fundamental horizon and refiguring the state as only one, possibly dispensable, vehicle for its realisation.
10.1177/07255136261487204.title: Inverting the triangle of power: The military–industrial complex after Silicon Valley

10.1177/07255136261487205.abstract: Geoeconomic competition has returned to the world polity. This paper compares the situation before the world wars to that of the contemporary world. The paper argues that war is not likely to result from geoeconomic competition—though war may well result from more traditional reasons.
10.1177/07255136261487205.title: The return of geoeconomics: How scared should we be?

10.1177/07255136261487456.abstract: Nick Land is a British philosopher who has been leading the Dark Enlightenment movement. This paper examines the philosophical foundations of Land's right-wing trajectory and asks how the digital is integrated into his political economy and anti-humanist worldview. It situates Land within a broader context in which contemporary crises of neoliberal capitalism coincide with authoritarian and neo-reactionary currents often grouped under the label ‘Dark Enlightenment’. The analysis reconstructs continuities between Land's early work and his post-2013 writings by identifying five characteristic motifs that constitute the TOXIC schema, a mnemonic for the five key features of Nick Land's thought: T, the termination of Kant's influence; O, opposition to universalism and humanism; X, xeno-capitalism; I, informatic transhumanism; C, capitalist accelerationism. The paper analyses these five features. Land's position on capitalism as an autonomous, cybernetic, self-organising machinic system, based on Deleuze and Guattari's works, makes his work attractive to Silicon Valley gurus. His xeno-capitalism is a model for authoritarian statecraft (CEO-monarchy and ‘exit’ politics), while informatic acceleration is a project of insulating techno-capital from democratic constraint. The result is a distinctive form of right-wing accelerationism that links digital capitalism to authoritarian political imaginaries.
10.1177/07255136261487456.title: The TOXIC schema: How Nick Land's Dark Enlightenment works

10.1177/07255136261487457.abstract: This article challenges the reduction of blockchain to an institutional technology for lowering transaction costs by interpreting it as an autopoietic system of operational closure. Drawing on Francisco Varela's theory of biological autonomy and Cornelius Castoriadis’ account of political autonomy, it distinguishes between functional autonomy, understood as systemic self-maintenance, and political autonomy, understood as collective self-institution. The article argues that blockchain governance is marked by a rigidity paradox: the deterministic mechanisms that secure trustless coordination also risk foreclosing the indeterminacy required for democratic deliberation. Through the cases of the Ethereum hard fork and KONG Land, the article shows how algorithmic consensus can produce a form of functional sovereignty while displacing the interpretive and instituting dimensions of law. It concludes by proposing the need to rethink decentralized governance as an open rather than closed autopoiesis.
10.1177/07255136261487457.title: Algorithmic autopoiesis and the operational closure of law: The performativity of consensus as the production of socio-political reality

10.1177/0725513696001045008.abstract: It could be conceivable that society is not an organism, that it has no structure, that it functions only temporarily or seemingly. The most obvious analogies are not the best. The Human Province, p.245 True, he [man] wants to “preserve” himself, but he also simultaneously wants other things which are inseparable from this. Crowds and Power, p. 293 The planning nature of man is a very late addition that violates his essential, his transforming nature. The Secret Heart of the Clock, p. 119 Man, regarding himself as the measure of all things, is almost unknown. His progress in self-knowledge is minimal, every new theory obscures more of him than it illuminates. The Conscience of Words, p. 111
10.1177/0725513696001045008.title: Canetti's Counter-image of Society

10.1177/0725513697049000005.abstract: Thinking the origin in a radical way amounts to thinking the movement by which what does not proceed from something else - what does not have its origin elsewhere - comes to itself, has within itself precisely the ontological energy to detach itself from itself and to exist as origin. In its primordial sense, then, origin is self-origin: it is, becomes, and is known starting from itself. This self-presupposition of the origin constitutes the very advent of Being, its unmotivated and permanent upsurge, which has to be thought in terms of creation. Human creation responds to this ontological genesis, to its indeterminacy and to its incompletion - and, consequently, to its temporality. At once individual and collective - that is, both psychical and social - human creation alone can give meaning to ontological genesis.
10.1177/0725513697049000005.title: The Self-Presupposition of the Origin: Homage to Cornelius Castoriadis

10.1177/0725513697050000005.abstract: In recent years Singapore has come to be seen as a successful project of economic transformation and capitalist development. What is more remarkable - but less discussed - is Singapore's success in building a multiethnic society and the unique concomitant civilizing processes that have accompanied this. Singapore represents today a project of a multi-ethnic and multi-cultural polity and a postmodern global city that combines civility, nostalgia and economic functionality. Here it is argued that - despite some well-known and decisive dark spots on the political landscape - this success has to do with two concomitant processes. One is the functionally administered extension of the state into the meaning-sphere of the individual, totalizing it from within his own nostalgia in an exoticized urban space. The other is the soteriological transcendence of individual and intra-individual relations within and beyond the culturally recognized `communities'. Westerners will not be able to learn from the Singapore process of multi-cultural civilization should they continue to merely understand it in terms of `Asian authoritarianism'.
10.1177/0725513697050000005.title: `Elias in Singapore': Civilizing Processes in a Tropical City

10.1177/0725513697051000002.abstract: The article sketches an approach to the sociology of the stranger which is based on historical semantics, on comparative studies of social structures of premodern societies and on a reconsideration of the `classical sociology of the stranger' and of marginality (Simmel, 1908; Michels, 1929 and others; Schütz, 1944; Park, 1964). The guiding hypothesis of the article is that there is a discontinuity in the modern experience of the stranger which has not been reflected sufficiently in the classical sociology of the stranger. Whereas in premodern societies membership criteria are binary codes such as `kin' vs. `stranger', `friend' vs. `enemy', and elaborate arrangements were then necessary for institutionalizing a third status (e.g. for internal strangers) between the binary alternatives, the modern experience is wholly different. Modern society is no longer a membership organization. The third status (i.e. being neither `friend' nor `stranger') has become constitutive of our everyday experience of other persons. And this everyday experience is that of indifference as our normal attitude towards most persons living in the world. A modern sociology of the stranger has to explore the facets of indifference. Indifference can be described as an interactional achievement in situations of fleeting contact. And it can be examined in its macrostructural consequences in a modern societal order in which motivations for societal engagements and therefore any willingness to care for the other are unavoidably scarce.
10.1177/0725513697051000002.title: The Stranger - on the Sociology of the Indifference

10.1177/0725513697051000004.abstract: The article inquires into the uneasiness of sociological systems theory about culture. Culture alternatively is called the solution to the problem of double contingency (Parsons) and removed from this solution (Luhmann). It is shown that meaning is the more basic term whose description reveals a form rule of social systems which is only patterned, yet not understood by culture. Culture is a memory and control device of society. It may be conceived of as providing the distinction of correct versus incorrect behaviour. But who decides on the correctness or incorrectness of this distinction? Sociological thinking takes off where the cultural and the social are distinguished.
10.1177/0725513697051000004.title: The Meaning of Culture

10.1177/0725513697051000005.abstract: As a universal theory Luhmann's systems theory of society includes art in its ambit. The Art of Society (1995) reconstructs the formal and the social-historical conditions of the functional differentiation of a system of art since the Renaissance. The methodological focus of the reconstruction - Luhmann's theory of form (perception, first and second order observation, medium and form) and of systemic differentiation (social function, self-organization, codes and programmes, evolution and self-description of art) - are analysed in the first part of the paper. The second part examines the unresolved question of the code of the art system, the hermeneutic circle integral to Luhmann's theory design, and the relation of his theory of art to the `aesthetic epoch' of art theory with special reference to Heidegger and Adorno.
10.1177/0725513697051000005.title: Paradox Preserved: From Ontology to Autology. Reflections on Niklas Luhmann's the Art of Society

10.1177/0725513698052000006.abstract: This paper argues that contemporary diasporic identities provide a strong basis from which to oppose contemporary expressions of racism. Immigrant and mobile populations have been able to construct images of identity that are based neither on an assimilationist model, nor defensive strategies against assimilationism. Rather, the older, internal relation between racism and diasporization has been broken by the ability of groups to claim a diasporic status on the basis of a public and not private articulation of self-identity.
10.1177/0725513698052000006.title: Racism and Diasporas

10.1177/0725513698054000004.abstract: Globalization cuts both ways. Not only does it valorize the local in a cultural sense, it constructs the local as the tribal. Processes of geopolitical fragmentation give those in power even more room to manoeuvre. Glocalization involves the reallocation of poverty and stigma from above without even the residual responsibility of noblesse oblige. Geographical and social mobility are dichotomized; populations are refigured as tourists and vagabonds. Globalization thus reinforces already existing patterns of domination, while globalization indicates trends to dispersal and conflict on neo-traditional grounds. The privileged walk, or fly away; the others take revenge upon each other.
10.1177/0725513698054000004.title: On Glocalization: or Globalization for some, Localization for some Others

10.1177/0725513698054000006.abstract: Unemployment in Europe is currently a major challenge. Two models for solving the problem are frequently proposed: a work model, which in its radical version institutes a legally binding right to employment, and a basic income model, which in its radical form establishes a universal, unconditional right to income security. In practice, western democracies have experimented with mixed forms of both models, with a greater emphasis on guaranteeing work. This article examines the justifications of these two models in their radical versions, with a special focus on the experience of self-respect. The conclusion is that the benefits that traditionally are associated with paid work function better in justifying a right to basic income than a right to work.
10.1177/0725513698054000006.title: The Social Basis of Self-Respect: A Normative Discussion of Politics Against Unemployment

10.1177/0725513698054000007.abstract: One reason for the problematic status of the social sciences is that their claim to legitimacy has been undermined by two opposite models of inquiry: the nomothetic idea of science, with its emphasis on universal laws, and the idiographic conception of history as a record of particular events. It can be argued that both of them excluded the temporal dimension of socio-historical reality; more precisely, they were ill-equipped to analyze the unstable structures which emerge and undergo transformations over varying periods of time. This previously excluded middle has been rediscovered by pioneering scientists on both sides of the divide; the paper compares Prigogine's critique of Newtonian natural science with Braudel's reorientation of history. The former line of argument privileges time, the latter duration, but they lead to similar conclusions.
10.1177/0725513698054000007.title: Time and Duration: The Unexcluded Middle, or Reflections on Braudel and Prigogine

10.1177/0725513699057000004.abstract: Students in 1989 were at pains to distinguish their actions from those taken by students in the Cultural Revolution. Yet there were important similarities. In the present paper, we identify influence on the Democracy Movement from the Cultural Revolution through (1) the expansion and/or widespread familiarization of repertories of collective action available to Chinese activists; (2) precedents for collective action that may have lowered the barriers to action for some while raising them for others; (3) the participation of people at different stages of their lives in both movements; (4) the transformation of the significance of the ideas of democracy and political authority wrought by the Cultural Revolution for many Chinese; (5) the impact of the Cultural Revolution on Chinese intellectuals; (6) the material consequences of the Cultural Revolution which contributed to China's position in the post-Mao era and the specific issues reform and protest sought to confront; (7) the discourse of corruption which provided the 1989 movement with its strongest links between students and ordinary citizens, and which was accentuated in the Cultural Revolution; (8) the affirmation of the value of ordinary life by which students in the 1980s, encouraged by the `literature of the wounded', rebelled against the Puritanism and denigration of `unauthorized' personal relationships that had been characteristic of the Cultural Revolution; (9) the role of the Cultural Revolution as a cautionary tale, shaping the movement itself, inhibiting some older intellectuals from participating, and determining much of how the government viewed and responded to the Democracy Movement; and (10) the embeddedness in different ways of both Cultural Revolution and 1989 protests in an international context.
10.1177/0725513699057000004.title: Legacies of Radicalism: China's Cultural Revolution and the Democracy Movement of 1989

10.1177/0725513699057000007.abstract: This article attempts to examine Nihonjinron, the popular essentialist genre in Japan, which purports to analyse Japan's quintessence and cultural core by using three concepts - nationality, ethnicity and culture - synonymously. The focus of the paper will be placed on: (1) the widespread political bases of Nihonjinron and its internal divisions; (2) its changing features in the face of globalization; (3) the possible productive uses of Nihonjinron at both conceptual and theoretical levels; and (4) the dilemma of inter-societal and intra-societal cultural relativism, which the Nihonjinron debate has highlighted. The paper presents an outline of an inductive, pluralistic, multicultural model of analysis as a possible alternative.
10.1177/0725513699057000007.title: Making Sense of Nihonjinron

10.1177/1474885102001001003.abstract: Given the rise in transnational problems and the inadequacy of the old, intergovernmental system, scholars are searching for a new, post-cold war global architecture. The 2001 anti-terrorism coalition presents a new architecture - the semi-empire - which is dominated by one nation (or a small group of nations) that pressures other nations to follow the course it sets, and has a limited number of missions. The article explores the possibility that the coalition could expand to tackle other transnational problems besides terrorism. Given the coalition's lack of scope and legitimacy, other options are explored that might be more effective and legitimate. The alternatives turn out to be either based on the old system (e.g. transgovernmental agencies), unrealistic except in the very long term (a global nation), or implausible (e.g. a global constitutional assembly). The article argues that an expanded coalition, or semi-empire, might gradually become more effective and legitimate over time.
10.1177/1474885102001001003.title: Implications of the American Anti-Terrorism Coalition for Global Architectures

10.1177/1474885102001001007.abstract: The history of concepts has partly replaced the older style of the `history of ideas' and can be extended to a critique of normative political theory and, thereby, understood as an indirect style of political theorizing. A common feature in Quentin Skinner's and Reinhart Koselleck's writings lies in their critique of the unhistorical and depoliticizing use of concepts. This concerns especially the classical contractarian theories, and both authors remark that this still holds for work by their contemporary heirs, such as Rawls, Habermas and other contemporary normative theorists. Conceptual history offers us a chance to turn the contestability, contingency and historicity of the use of concepts into instruments for conceptualizing politics. The alternative, indirect mode of political theorizing Skinner and Koselleck practise consists of a `Verfremdungseffekt', which helps us to distance ourselves from thinking in terms of contemporary paradigms, unquestioned conventions, given constellations of alternatives or implicit value judgements. In the Skinnerian variant the conceptual changes are made intelligible through analysis of the rhetorical redescriptions among the political agents, whereas Koselleck thematizes the differences in the temporal index of concepts. The subversive aspect in the history of concepts consists of the explication and historical variation of the tacit normative content in the use of concepts.
10.1177/1474885102001001007.title: The History of Concepts as a Style of Political Theorizing: Quentin Skinner's and Reinhart Koselleck's Subversion of Normative Political Theory

10.1177/1474885102001002004.abstract: This article analyses the reception of John Rawls's thought by Otfried Höffe, Jürgen Habermas and other political theorists on the German liberal left. It argues that, ironically, as Rawls's theory has become more historically self-conscious and sociologically oriented since A Theory of Justice, Habermas, while denying any fundamental difference between him and Rawls in this `neo-Kantian family quarrel', has moved in the opposite direction. One might even say that there has been some mid-Atlantic convergence in political theory. Nevertheless, there remain peculiarities of German political thought, in particular its more sociological bent, a (positive or negative) fixation on the state, and the persistently felt need finally to reconcile a perceived conflict between liberalism and democracy.
10.1177/1474885102001002004.title: Rawls in Germany

10.1177/1474885103002001277.abstract: This article discusses the normative implications of the European integration process by addressing the question of the legitimacy deficit in the EU and its member states. It starts from an analysis of legitimacy as implying a distinction between `polity' and `regime', each of which has an `internal' and an `external' dimension relating respectively to the subjective perceptions of citizens and to more objective- and universalist-oriented criteria. Standard accounts of the integration process and the constitutionalisation of the EU have overlooked the complex ways in which polity- and regime-building interact. They have also emphasized the external legitimacy of the EU while neglecting the internal dimension. Both descriptively and prescriptively, the EU lies in between the interpretations offered by neofunctionalist or intergovernmental realists and federal idealists. The `internal' norms channelled through the EU's `regime' have helped form the economic interests appealed to by the former, but in rather different ways to that assumed by the latter. The result has been a polycentric `polity' with a multi-level `regime'. Consequently, we reject having either an EU written constitution that goes beyond the treaties or a federal legislature, advocating instead the `republican' model of a `mixed commonwealth'.
10.1177/1474885103002001277.title: Legitimizing the Euro-`polity' and its `Regime': The Normative Turn in EU Studies

10.1177/1474885103002001280.abstract: Within feminist commentary, there has been increasing disillusionment with the radical feminist thesis commonly associated with the work of Catharine MacKinnon. Set against the backdrop of this disillusionment, this article traces the development of an emerging genre of contemporary feminist critique, which has been heavily influenced by the writings of French genealogist Michel Foucault. The work of Foucault, despite focusing upon issues of power and sexuality that have long since been central to the radical feminist project, appears to offer a stark alternative to the accompanying radical feminist emphasis upon grand-scale theories of domination and gender-based victimization. Highlighting the points of divergence between Foucault and radical feminism, this article joins with much contemporary feminist commentary in heralding the Foucaultian position as a worthy alternative, capable of remedying the problems of essentialism and determinism that have plagued MacKinnon's arguments. Unlike much contemporary feminist commentary, however, this article also seeks to highlight the similarities between the theoretical positions of MacKinnon and Foucault. With a particular focus upon Foucault's work on domination, this article charts the reinsertion of asymmetrical power relationships within the Foucaultian landscape, and highlights the impact of that development upon popular understandings of his thesis on micro-politics, bio-power and resistance. Locating the centrality of domination to Foucault's thesis on power, the article will re-establish the relevance of related aspects of that analysis for the purposes of contemporary feminist critique.
10.1177/1474885103002001280.title: On Power and Domination: Feminism and the Final Foucault

10.1177/1474885103002003003.abstract: The article deals with Habermas's intersubjective approach to critical social theory, focusing on his intersubjective accounts of truth, justice and democratic legitimacy. Distinguishing between stronger and weaker versions of an intersubjective account, it draws attention to Habermas's recent move from a strong intersubjective, constructivist, interpretation of truth to a weaker, non-constructivist, one. It then looks at his refusal to make a similar move in the case of justice, arguing that it is not well-founded, even from the point of view of Habermas's overall concerns. It contends, in particular, that a strong intersubjective conception is not necessary in order to maintain the close link between normative validity and argumentation that plays an important role in Habermas's project of a critical social theory and concludes that the advantages of abandoning a strong intersubjective position outweigh the disadvantages. Consequently, it recommends extension of the weaker, non-constructivist, account that Habermas now proposes in the case of truth to justice as well. In the final section, it considers the implications of this recommendation for Habermas's conception of normative validity in the domain of law and politics.
10.1177/1474885103002003003.title: The Weaknesses of Strong Intersubjectivism: Habermas's Conception of Justice

10.1177/1474885103002003005.abstract: The purpose of this article is to discuss the type of attachment and allegiance propounded in the recently proclaimed Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union. Charters such as Bills of Rights are generally held to be reflective of and evocative of a rights-based constitutional patriotism. The EU is not a state; there are widely different conceptions of what it is and should be, one of which is the vision of a Europe of nation states. Is the spirit of the Charter thus instead that of deep diversity, i.e. reflective of a wide diversity of views, visions and values as to what the EU is and ought to be? The article contrasts constitutional patriotism and deep diversity as alternative underlying philosophies of the Charter and also briefly examines the Charter's presumed ability to produce either type of sentiment of allegiance.
10.1177/1474885103002003005.title: The European Union: In Search of an Identity

10.1177/14748851030024005.abstract: Central to his own fruitful study of modern society and politics, of the stakes and twists-and-turns of the dramatic twentieth century, was Raymond Aron's fifty year engagement with `Marx and Marxism'. In a series of lecture courses (and elsewhere) Aron provided a comprehensive, balanced, and judicious exposition and appreciation of Marx's intellectual itinerary. On one hand, Marx helpfully highlighted various tensions in liberal-bourgeois society. On the other hand, however, his apolitical, materialistic explanations of them and, especially, his prediction of capitalism's explosive self-overcoming proved grossly inadequate. In addition to being a special sort of social scientist, Marx was a Promethean humanist who rejected all natural and social limits and who claimed to scientifically predict the coming of the true and real City of Man. Aron's own `balanced social analysis' and his humane, sober, reformist thought stand in stark contrast.
10.1177/14748851030024005.title: Aron, Marx, and Marxism: An Interpretation

10.1177/1474885104041048.abstract: The objective of this article is to contribute to an understanding of Hannah Arendt’s special place in present-day political theory by means of a contrast between her Origins of Totalitarianism and four important political science studies of National Socialism and totalitarianism, three written by authors who shared the status of involuntary emigrant with Arendt, that are offered as constituting the original context of her work. A critical appreciation of the seminal works by Ernst Fraenkel, Franz L. Neumann, Sigmund Neumann, and Carl Joachim Friedrich and Zbigniew Brezinski, with special emphasis on questions of method, opens the way to a reconsideration of the distinctly philosophical character of Arendt’s work, and its shocking challenges to the scientific orientations of political science.
10.1177/1474885104041048.title: Hannah Arendt’s The Origins of Totalitarianism in its Original Context

10.1177/1474885104045911.abstract: This article interprets David Hume’s social and political thought as a ‘theory of civil society’, arguing that as such it constituted an important challenge to the civic humanism of much early 18th-century British political argument. Since republican theorists invoke the historical traditions of civic thought in current debates, Hume’s theory of civil society therefore is of especial interest in relation to the foundations of contemporary neo-republicanism. The first part argues that, in A Treatise of Human Nature, by analysing various different kinds of relation between human beings, Hume articulated a fundamental distinction between society and the state. The second examines Hume’s Essays and Political Discourses, focusing in particular on the relationship between the respective interests of society and government, the effects of commercial refinement on virtues and sociability, and on forms of mediation between society and the state. The concluding section reviews the historical and theoretical significance of Hume’s theory, focusing particularly on concepts of liberty.
10.1177/1474885104045911.title: Hume’s Theory of Civil Society

10.1177/1474885104045914.abstract: This article critically examines Jürgen Habermas’s theory of democracy as developed in Between Facts and Norms. In particular, it focuses on the concept of communicative power and argues that there is a crucial ambiguity in Habermas’s use of this concept. Since communicative power is the key normative resource that is supposed to counter the norm-free steering media of money and administrative power, its role within the theory must be made clear. The article begins by explaining the normative and social-theoretic foundations of the theory. Then it highlights the normative importance of the public sphere in Habermas’s two-track model of deliberative politics, before turning to the problems with the concept of communicative power. Two alternative readings of its role are provided in order to demonstrate how it needs to be further clarified.
10.1177/1474885104045914.title: Communicative Power in Habermas’s Theory of Democracy

10.1177/1474885105050449.abstract: This article is a study of the trajectory of the contemporary French liberal philosopher Marcel Gauchet from his early, ‘anarchist’ commitments through the 1970s to his discovery and defense of liberalism, notably as expressed in his 1980 revival and interpretation of his 19th-century countryman Benjamin Constant’s post-revolutionary liberalism. Discussed in the article are Gauchet’s devotion to and revision of the portrait of primitive society he inherited from the French anthropologist Pierre Clastres, how his early political and theoretical concerns are transmuted in Gauchet’s reading of Constant, and the relevance of this trajectory for comprehending even Gauchet’s most recent pronouncements about the nature and future of liberal society.
10.1177/1474885105050449.title: Savage and Modern Liberty: Marcel Gauchet and the Origins of New French Thought

10.1177/1474885105050450.abstract: This article argues that Camus’s thinking, as expressed in his works of fiction and non-fiction, is based upon a contradiction between his determination to reconcile politics and ethics and his belief that they irrefutably contradict each other. Throughout his career, Camus’s concerns never diverged from his aporetic attempt to reach an ‘agreement’ between two concepts he regarded as incompatible: justice and freedom. This article demonstrates how this basic aporia led Camus to an original - albeit rather hopeless - view of the human condition. It illustrates how Camus’s aporia led him to define the role of thinkers in terms of public criticism and argues that in today’s sociopolitical reality Camus’s aporia can neither be dismissed, nor overcome.
10.1177/1474885105050450.title: Justice or Freedom: Camus’s Aporia

10.1177/1474885105052703.abstract: It has been argued recently that tyranny is a persisting phenomenon very much alive today, a greater danger than newer forms of misrule such as totalitarianism. One argument is based on human nature being such that the temptation to abuse political power in the form of tyranny remains a possibility in all societies. Another defines tyranny as a spiritual disorder of the soul and polity. Both date the 19th century as the time when tyranny dropped out of the western political vocabulary. In this view, modern political thought, like political science generally, has been impoverished by ignorance of, or indifference to, the nature of tyranny. By contrast, I treat tyranny not as possessing an essential, unchanging nature, but as a contested political concept used for a variety of purposes by different regimes and groups. Nor do I agree that, because ‘tyranny’ was used infrequently during the 19th century, systematic abuses of political power went unnoticed and unclassified. I treat a number of cases by postulating a family of controversial and contested regime types: tyranny, despotism, absolute monarchy, Bonapartism, Caesarism, and dictatorship. From them I conclude that, after tyranny was conflated with despotism at the end of the 18th century, both concepts were redescribed in terms of newer classifications belonging to the same conceptual family. Because ‘tyranny’ was then extended to many non-political arenas, it became so trivialized as to leave no prospect of our retrieving its once potent political meanings. If ‘tyranny’ is equally applicable to teachers, husbands, fashions, or public opinion, the concept has lost its political cutting edge. It now lacks any distinctive meaning that might frame a situation and define it as calling for urgent and decisive action, especially in foreign policy.
10.1177/1474885105052703.title: A Family of Political Concepts: Tyranny, Despotism, Bonapartism, Caesarism, Dictatorship, 1750-1917

10.1177/1474885105052705.abstract: This article aims to examine the problem of political representation through the work of Lefort, Gauchet and Rosanvallon. It first looks at Lefort, who argues that a democratic society is characterized by a tension between its abstract guiding principles and its concrete reality. Political representation, then, mediates between these principles and society. This theory of representation allows Lefort, Gauchet and Rosanvallon not only to examine critically both past and present discourses of their contemporaries, but also to offer an alternative history of their own. Yet, since the 1980s, increasing individualization has exacerbated the tension between abstract principles and society, thus making political mediation more difficult. This article discusses the diagnosis and remedy to this predicament, as developed by Gauchet and Rosanvallon. While Gauchet offers an interesting diagnosis, but remains sceptical about possible solutions, Rosanvallon is more voluntarist and offers concrete solutions for today’s crisis of political representation.
10.1177/1474885105052705.title: Freedom through Political Representation: Lefort, Gauchet and Rosanvallon on the Relationship between State and Society

10.1177/1474885106059070.abstract: This article examines William Morris’s idea of Englishness, considered through a critique of his concept of fellowship or community. It looks at the charge that Morris wrongly neglected the importance of nationality as a focus for organization in socialism, preferring instead an internationalist ideal, based on an unworkable model of small-scale community. I defend Morris against these claims by arguing that Morris’s socialism was consistent with expressions of nationality and that his communitarianism was grounded on a concept of enjoyable labour, not friendship as is often supposed.
10.1177/1474885106059070.title: William Morris and the Problem of Englishness

10.1177/1474885106064663.abstract: This article uses Rousseau’s little-known responses to the Abbé de Saint-Pierre’s Project for Perpetual Peace and his fragments on ‘The State of War’ as a foil for Rawls’s claim that the international society he envisions in The Law of Peoples constitutes a ‘realistic utopia’. The main conclusion is that in a post-9/11 world Rousseau may have more to teach us about the possibilities for international security than Rawls does, since Rousseau’s theory accounts for the moral corruptibility of both individuals and groups. Most of the article focuses on comparing Rousseau’s and Rawls’s assumptions about human nature, but the final section also includes a brief discussion of their contrasting views of reason and the common good. The two philosophers agree, however, that the possibilities for international justice can only evolve out of the careful practice of local justice
10.1177/1474885106064663.title: Rousseau versus Rawls on International Relations

10.1177/1474885106064664.abstract: Representative democracy is often assessed from the standpoint of direct democracy. Recently, however, many theorists have come to argue that representation forms a democratic model in its own right. The most powerful claim in this direction is to be found within two quite different strands of thinking: the aesthetic theory of Frank Ankersmit and the savage theory of Claude Lefort. In this article, I show that while Ankersmit and Lefort converge in their critique of direct rule, they provide us with two distinct models of democracy. Aesthetic democracy, I argue, in the end falls short as a democratic recuperation of representation. It reduces representation to delegation. Savage democracy proves more fruitful in this respect. It offers a representative view of politics without committing itself to the premises associated with political delegation
10.1177/1474885106064664.title: Representative Democracy as Tautology: Ankersmit and Lefort on Representation

10.1177/1474885106067277.abstract: The purpose of this article is to explore the relationship between revolution and violence in Marxism and in a series of texts drawing on Marxian theory. Part 1 outlines the basic normative frameworks which determine the outer limits of permissible violence in Marxism. Part 2 presents a critical analysis of a series of later discussions - by Sorel, Fanon and Žižek - which transformed the terms in which violence was discussed by developing one particular aspect of Marxist thought. By teasing out the implications of revolutionary theory for the commission and permission of violence, it is possible to specify those points at which it tends towards excess. This in turn points towards limits that an adequate normative theory of revolutionary violence should establish.
10.1177/1474885106067277.title: Violence and Revolutionary Subjectivity: Marx to Žižek

10.1177/1474885107077311.abstract: Struggles for recognition are at the same time struggles over what it means to recognize and be recognized. Nancy Fraser and Axel Honneth propose two mutually exclusive ways to understand recognition: either as a matter of justice (Fraser) or as a matter of identity (Honneth). This article argues against the limitations of both of these construals of recognition, and offers a third way of construing it: as a matter of freedom. Recognition is not reducible, empirically or normatively, to any of these, however. Moreover, it needs to be regarded both more critically and more openly since what we are dealing with is a practice and an ideal that is by its very nature deeply contestable and therefore (more than most practices and ideals) subject to unforeseeable historical and normative change. Rather than trying to fix the meaning of recognition in order to give it a determinate role in ambitious theories of justice, it would be better to proceed more sceptically, attentive both to the complexities of recognition relations and to alternative ways of conceiving them and going on with them differently from before.
10.1177/1474885107077311.title: Struggling over the Meaning of Recognition: A Matter of Identity, Justice, or Freedom?

10.1177/1474885107077319.abstract: In this article I reply to four critics. Responding to Linda Alcoff, I contend that my original two-dimensional framework discloses the entwinement of economic and cultural strands of subordination, while also illuminating the dangers of identity politics. Responding to James Bohman, I maintain that, with the addition of the third dimension of representation, my approach illuminates the structural exclusion of the global poor, the relation between justice and democracy, and the status of comprehensive theorizing. Responding to Nikolas Kompridis, I defend a view of recognition that prioritizes the critique of institutionalized injustice. Responding to Rainer Forst, I argue that such a critique is better formulated in participation-theoretic than justification-theoretic terms.
10.1177/1474885107077319.title: Identity, Exclusion, and Critique: A Response to Four Critics

10.1177/1474885107080646.abstract: Benhabib argues that the tension between universal human rights and democratic self-determination cannot be resolved. Distinguishing between the principle of rights, on the one hand, and context-specific `schedules of rights', on the other hand, helps, however, to specify the scope of both norms.
