As the House Ethics Manual put it recently, it is of concern simply when an officeholder “cash[es] in on official position,” regardless of whether his or her official performance was in any way impaired as a result. Although the question of private gain from public office is richly implicative of a number of fundamental issues in political theory—in particular the ongoing controversy over where to draw the borders between private and public as well as the nature of official fiduciary responsibility—it has yet to undergo political-theoretic analysis. In what follows, I examine both the conceptual and normative issues emergent in the debate over private gain from public office.
10.2307/2952262.title: Beyond Quid Pro Quo: What's Wrong with Private Gain from Public Office?

10.2307/2952264.abstract: This paper investigates the dynamics of the “wasted vote” phenomenon and Duverger's Law. I construct a theoretical model in order to consider how preelection polls serve to inform the electorate about the relative chances of the candidates and how that information acts over time to decrease the support of the trailing candidate. The results shed light on how public opinion polls can aggregate information in the electorate and coordinate voters on the viable candidates in the election. Specifically, I show that in a Bayesian game model of strategic voting there exist non-Duvergerian equilibria in which all three candidates receive votes (in the limit). These equilibria require extreme coordination, however, and any variation in beliefs leads voters away from them to one of the Duvergerian equilibria. Thus, non-Duvergerian equilibria are unstable, while two-party equilibria are not. In addition, I describe how preelection polls provide information to voters about the viability of candidates and can thus be used by voters to coordinate on a Duvergerian outcome.
10.2307/2952264.title: Stability and Coordination in Duverger's Law: A Formal Model of Preelection Polls and Strategic Voting

10.2307/2952341.title: Local Commons and Global Interdependence: Heterogeneity and Cooperation in Two Domains. Edited by Robert O. Keohane and Elinor Ostrom. London: Sage Publications, 1995. 261p. $75.00 cloth, $21.95 paper.

10.2307/2952354.abstract: This paper develops a game-theoretic approach to the problem of political officials' respect for political and economic rights of citizens. It models the policing of rights as a coordination problem among citizens, but one with asymmetries difficult to resolve in a decentralized manner. The paper shows that democratic stability depends on a self-enforcing equilibrium: It must be in the interests of political officials to respect democracy's limits on their behavior. The concept of self-enforcing limits on the state illuminates a diverse set of problems and thus serves as a potential basis for integrating the literature. The framework is applied to a range of topics, such as democratic stability, plural societies, and elite pacts. The paper also applies its lessons to the case of the Glorious Revolution in seventeenth-century England.
10.2307/2952354.title: The Political Foundations of Democracy and the Rule of the Law

10.2307/2952355.abstract: Recently, the idea of phronesis has assumed great importance among political theorists. This prominence is due to the perception that, contrary to the application of the methods of natural science to politics, phronesis preserves the distinctive character of politics in its refusal to apply inappropriate standards of precision and to find certainty where it does not exist. But precisely because of this, the following question arises: Can we ascertain a nonarbitrary standard of phronesis without denying those characteristics that make it appropriate for the understanding of politics? I address this question by considering the treatment of phronesis (wisdom) found in Plato's Statesman and, in particular, the passage that weighs the relative merits of rule by wisdom and rule by law. In this seminal consideration of phronesis Plato (unlike Aristotle) does not confine his treatment to the practical sphere; even this intensely political passage contains far-reaching reflections on the nature of humanity and the world we inhabit. These explain what we are and what our world is, such that there is a need for this cognitive capacity. As I argue, they express the conditions of phronesis that can provide a guide for its use without negating its essential character.
10.2307/2952355.title: The Rule of Wisdom and the Rule of Law in Plato'sStatesman

10.2307/2952357.abstract: Is cooperation without central authority stable? If so, how robust is it? Despite what might be the conventional wisdom, The Evolution of Cooperation did not solve this problem deductively. In fact, results obtained later by others seem to have contradicted the book's main message. Reexamining this exceptionally influential work yields a new picture. Part of Axelrod's evolutionary story turns out to be false. But the main intuition, that retaliatory strategies of conditional cooperation are somehow advantaged, proves correct in one specific and significant sense: Under a standard evolutionary dynamic these strategies require the minimal frequency to stabilize. Hence, they support the most robust evolutionary equilibrium: the easiest to reach and retain. Moreover, the less efficient a strategy, the larger is its minimal stabilizing frequency; Hobbesian strategies of pure defection are the least robust. Our main theorems hold for a large class of games that pose diverse cooperation problems: prisoner's dilemma, chicken, stag hunt, and many others.
10.2307/2952357.title: The Evolutionary Stability of Cooperation

10.2307/2952359.abstract: A critical element of decision making is the timing of choices political actors make; often when a decision is made is as critical as the decision itself. We posit a dynamic model of strategic position announcement based on signaling theories of legislative politics. We suggest that members who receive clear signals from constituents, interest groups, and policy leaders will announce their positions earlier. Those with conflicting signals will seek more information, delaying their announcement. We test several expectations by examining data on when members of the House of Representatives announced their positions on the North American Free Trade Agreement. We also contrast the timing model with a vote model, and find that there are meaningful differences between the factors influencing the timing of position announcements and vote choice. Our research allows analysts to interpret the process leading up to the House action and the end state of that process.
10.2307/2952359.title: The Strategic Timing of Position Taking in Congress: A Study of the North American Free Trade Agreement

10.2307/2952360.abstract: In this work I test the proposition that normative standards of behavior can influence state actions in security-related conflicts. Specifically, I examine the construction of norms in the settlements of security-related disputes and the effects these settlements have on subsequent militarized interactions. I argue that dispute settlements alter subsequent crisis bargaining in two important ways. First, they act as normative referents that alter the interpretation of subsequent crisis bargaining behavior both by identifying a solution to the dispute which alleviates fears of demands for future concessions and by defining a set of acts which both sides consider illegitimate. Second, in combination with the response to their violation, dispute settlements inflict reputational costs on states that violate them. I test these arguments against a realist theory of crisis bargaining through an analysis of 122 reinitiated international crises between 1929 and 1979. I find strong support for the hypothesis that states can and do construct normative standards that guide their behavior in international crises, whereas realist theory receives only mixed support.
10.2307/2952360.title: Crime and Punishment: The Role of Norms in Crisis Bargaining

10.2307/2952362.abstract: This study uses regression analysis of data from a telephone survey of 380 married couples to subject to rare empirical test the contention that, because women are unequal at home, they cannot be equal in the polity. The argument is often made that wives' disadvantage in comparison to their husbands with respect to control over family income, availability of free time, power over decisions, or mutual respect dampens their ability to participate fully in politics. In fact, domestic inequalities do have implications for political activity, but these effects differ from what is usually posited by being stronger for husbands than for wives. For husbands, control over major financial decisions and autonomy in using small amounts of time enhance their ability to participate in politics beyond what would be expected on the basis of their other characteristics. In short, being boss at home is politically empowering to husbands.
10.2307/2952362.title: The Public Consequences of Private Inequality: Family Life and Citizen Participation

10.53765/20512988.44.4.705.abstract: This paper investigates Herbert Spencer's influence on William Stanley Jevons' political thought. Jevons' thought was shaped by three ideas, which can be traced back to Spencer: the idea that individuals were no tabula rasa ; the belief that evolution was a beneficent process; and the idea that moral sentiment evolved towards perfection. I will also show why Jevons supported the idea of interventionist social reform, which Spencer rejected, and I will argue that this disagreement stemmed from Jevons' commitment to Jeremy Bentham's utilitarianism.
10.53765/20512988.44.4.705.title: The Instruments of Evolution: Herbert Spencer's Influence on William Stanley Jevons' Political Thought

10.53765/20512988.44.4.781.abstract: I view Don Quixote as a representative of Eric Nelson's 'Greek' view of freedom and Sancho Panza as an embodiment of Quentin Skinner's 'neo-Roman' view. Each has their worldview challenged by their adventures such that their view- points become reversed by the climax of the novel. I point to the Greek tradition's entanglement in the Spanish conquest of the Americas as a reason Cervantes would wish to divest his main character of the Greek view. Accordingly, I suggest that the concept of penance plays a crucial role in how the author positions the rival traditions in relation to Spanish history.
10.53765/20512988.44.4.781.title: The Rival Freedoms of Don Quixote

10.53765/20512988.45.1.124.abstract: Hegel saw freedom not primarily as a property of the individual’s will, but of a totality (from which individual freedom is metaphysically derived). This aspect of Hegel’s political theory stemmed from his attempt to construct a state that could foster a renewal of Christian spirituality. This project had to confront the fragmentation of the Holy Roman Empire, which Hegel attributed to the self-interestedness of its component parts. This historical case for the priority of the whole over its parts, however, was soon supplanted by a philosophical argument for a political totality whose freedom entailed its subordination of conflicting parts within itself.
10.53765/20512988.45.1.124.title: Freedom and Totality: How Hegel Became Hegel

10.53765/20512988.45.2.205.abstract: This article challenges the common representation of the Stoics as apolitical – that is, interested in neither the philosophical nor the practical aspects of political life. Instead, they are said to have turned away from politics and the state towards internal psychic management and the achievement of the ideal mental states of apatheia and ataraxia . We contest this standard account of Stoicism in four ways. First, we present bibliographic evidence that testifies to the Stoics’ longstanding interest in politics. Second, we show that the Stoics insisted that the good life necessitated service to others and this expressly included political service. Third, we explore how Stoic cosmopolitanism provided a potent doctrinal challenge to the particularism of antiquity, with radical implications for how we should conceive and discharge our political duties. Fourth, we demonstrate how the Stoic pursuit of ataraxia (tranquillity) and apatheia (detachment) were methods of internal regulation profoundly connected to external political duties and action.
10.53765/20512988.45.2.205.title: Were the Stoics Apolitical?

10.53765/20512988.45.2.229.abstract: Baptism is a theological and religious sacrament by which individuals become Christians. This article shows that in medieval and renaissance law, baptism was also a civil legal event which could grant civilitas . From the Siete Partidas onwards, baptism was taken to be a legitimate origin of natural obligations within a community. As jurists like Lucas de Penna bridged the legal gap between spiritual matters ( spiritualia ) and temporal matters ( temporalia ), jurists and theorists alike could argue that baptism ought to change one’s legal origin ( patria or origo ) or liberate them from certain civic obligations while contracting them into others. Only by tracing how baptism came to have civil and legal significance can we then understand how participants in political communities leveraged the obligations created through baptismal oaths against tyrants, kings, bishops and their fellow civic-members.
10.53765/20512988.45.2.229.title: Baptism and Civic-Membership in Medieval and Early Modern Law

10.53765/20512988.45.2.257.abstract: This article offers a novel interpretation of Robert Filmer’s political thought. I argue that, rather than identifying kings with biological fathers, Filmer bases his theory on a distinctive conception of fatherhood as a right of dominium and on a distinction between ordinary and ‘supreme’ fatherhood. I show that he only fully develops this theory in the second manuscript version of Patriarcha through an engagement with Grotius and Selden and that these ideas distinguish him from other early Stuart patriarchal thinkers. The article also analyses how his views on tyranny, usurpation, and forms of government evolve in relevant ways over time, identifying a shift in his position from a de facto theory of authority to a de facto theory of obedience.
10.53765/20512988.45.2.257.title: ‘Full of Contradiction, or Confusion, or Both’: Rethinking the Political Thought of Robert Filmer

10.53765/20512988.45.2.282.abstract: This article explores the current post-colonial critique of Locke, which is primarily based on a Macphersonian proto-capitalist interpretation of Locke’s theory of unlimited property rights. It explores Locke’s Two Treatises , his economic essays on interest rates and his colonial proposal on Virginia’s administrative defects. I contend that Locke provides a theory of limited property rights which rejects over-accumulation of money and land because it might lead to political subjection to arbitrary power. My analysis helps to explain how and to what extent Locke’s colonial accounts of Virginia reflect his theory of limited property rights embodied in the Two Treatises .
10.53765/20512988.45.2.282.title: A Limited Colonialist and not an Imperialist: Revisiting Locke’s Account of Property Rights

10.53765/20512988.45.2.305.abstract: Rousseau appears to condemn amour-propre as a whole for producing harmful relations of dependence and psychic division. However, recent interpreters have called this traditional view into question and argued that amour-propre can in fact have several beneficial expressions for Rousseau. This article treats the Emile ’s account of anger, one neglected expression of amour-propre that displays its potential to uphold moral freedom when educated into autonomous pride. Attention to this passion reveals that Rousseau’s treatment of amour-propre poses a challenge to a tradition of Christian suspicion towards pride. Rousseau’s analysis of self-love is rooted in a fundamental reversal of the Augustinian distinction between harmful and beneficial amour-propre , a reversal which exculpates a form of human pride that the Augustinians condemned.
10.53765/20512988.45.2.305.title: In Defence of Pride: Rousseau’s Challenge to the Augustinians

10.53765/20512988.45.2.327.abstract: This article seeks to understand the possibility of moral improvement in human social history through a close interpretation of Kant’s A Renewed Attempt to Answer the Question: Is the Human Race Continually Improving? The article examines the ways in which Kant’s arguments in this final piece, while often overlooked, complicate his philosophy of history as put forward in earlier works. Through this comparison, one sees important complications in Kant’s thoughts on the philosophy of history at the end of his career, conceding that rightful progress towards a global republicanism is the most we can be sure of. This concession is striking considering Kant’s ambitious goal at the outset to demonstrate the theoretical certainty of moral progress, going well beyond the practical optimism he advocates in earlier works. Yet, despite this concession, Kant is still optimistic about the possibility of moral progress at the end of the piece. This article suggests that Kant’s Renewed Attempt is best understood as a window into Kant’s grappling with the difficulties of constructing a philosophy of history that is consistent with his moral philosophy. By doing so, the text reveals underappreciated complexities of Kant’s practical thought.
10.53765/20512988.45.2.327.title: Is Progress Possible? Moral Improvement in Kant’s Renewed Attempt

10.53765/20512988.45.2.347.abstract: Alexis de Tocqueville’s intellectual legacy has been characterized in terms of an arc: instant celebrity upon the publication of Democracy in America followed by waning influence after his death and belated rediscovery in the latter half of the twentieth century. Yet this article argues that Tocqueville’s ideas remained influential in the fin-de-siècle writings of the syndicalist Georges Sorel. It explores the curious matter of how a liberal famed for his commitment to a juste milieu in French politics could have played a significant role in the thinking of a radical defender of proletarian violence. Beyond the ideological curiosity of their interconnection, it demonstrates that the lessons Sorel derives from Tocqueville effectively transform a conservative argument about the futility of political revolutions into a call for structural upheaval. Sorel’s attention to these and other elements of Tocqueville’s political theory, we conclude, complicates further the ‘strange’ nature of the latter’s liberalism.
10.53765/20512988.45.2.347.title: Georges Sorel’s Tocqueville

10.53765/20512988.45.2.372.abstract: The Cambridge School of the history of political thought exists as a tradition of teaching in the History Faculty of Cambridge University, and as a set of works including famous books such as The Political Thought of John Locke , The Machiavellian Moment and The Foundations of Modern Political Thought . It acquired its distinctive status because of three methodological articles written in the 1960s by the triumvirate of J.G.A. Pocock, John Dunn and Quentin Skinner. These articles are usually assimilated to each other. No doubt there was much consonance between the three articles. But I demonstrate through a close reading of the three articles that each author placed a very different emphasis on the status and purpose of the history of political thought, and that the differences between the articles help to explain the remarkable differences in the subsequent writings of the authors from the late 1960s onwards. This article is not part of the recent tendency to study the thought of the last fifty years historically, though it may of course be a preliminary to that. My concern is textual, not contextual. This article should interest anyone concerned with the question of the relevance of historiography, the history of ideas and the history of political thought to the study of politics.
10.53765/20512988.45.2.372.title: The Triumvirate of the Cambridge School: Pocock’s, Dunn’s and Skinner’s Methodological Articles on the History of Political Thought, 1962‐1969

10.53765/20512988.45.3.425.abstract: In Natural Reason and Natural Law , James Carey states that, for Aquinas, the good is pursued necessarily as according to the first principle of practical reason, but then makes the stunning admission that humans really seem to almost always pursue 'the best'. Such an admission opens Thomistic natural law to an attack from the Socratic paradox that all evil stems from ignorance, a philosophical premise that implicitly undermines all moral responsibility. While Carey and others consider Aquinas' position as ultimately defensible, they nowhere consider its Socratic articulation. This paper therefore offers a new analysis of Aquinas' rejection of Socrates' paradox.
10.53765/20512988.45.3.425.title: Aquinas on the Socratic Paradox and the Problem of Virtue

10.53765/20512988.45.4.758.abstract: This article explores John Stuart Mill's career-long interest in federal models of politics. Demonstrating how Mill's multi-faceted account was shaped by his understanding of civilization and empire, it argues that Mill was far more committed to federalism — as historical phenomenon, solution to contemporary political crises, and ideal for the future organization of humanity — than is usually recognized. From his readings of ancient Greek history, through his reflection on the United States constitution, to his musing on the fate of Europe and the British colonial system, federalism formed an important part of Mill's vision of politics, past, present and future.
10.53765/20512988.45.4.758.title: John Stuart Mill on Federation, Civilization and Empire

10.53765/20512988.46.1.133.abstract: This is the first of two articles analysing the intellectual formation of Alfred Zimmern, a leading figure in the study of International Relations in the first half of the twentieth century. Drawing on many archival sources, it argues against claims in recent scholarship that Zimmern was strongly influenced by the Idealism popular at Oxford at the time he read Literae Humaniores . Instead, it sets Zimmern’s concerns in the context of the emerging social sciences and argues that it was the study of Ancient History rather than Philosophy that shaped his early internationalist thought. The article as a whole studies disciplinary methodology in the writing of intellectual history.
10.53765/20512988.46.1.133.title: Alfred Zimmern’s Early Political Thought I: Idealism, Internationalism and the Study of Ancient History

10.53765/20512988.46.4.587.abstract: Plato’s Seventh Letter contains a digression on the philosopher as a wise and unheard adviser. Through this digression, it is possible to see the entire letter as a representation of the philosophical activity addressed mainly to non-philosophers. While commentaries on the letter have generally focused on the signs of its authenticity, this paper proposes to read it considering the activity of political counselling through three distinct sections of the text. In this way, we get a new insight into the problem of the letter’s composition and discover an important and lasting aspect of the philosopher’s political self-representation within the Platonic tradition.
10.53765/20512988.46.4.587.title: The Philosopher as a Political Adviser: A New Reading of Plato’s Seventh Letter

10.53765/20512988.46.4.604.abstract: Despite extensive discussion of Locke’s consent theory of political obligations, it remains unclear how Locke sustains inter-generational allegiance, i.e. the reproduction of widespread membership among the native-born children of members. This article attempts to fill this gap by reconsidering Locke’s expectation that membership is required for the inheritance of property. For Locke, foreigners are permitted to naturalize or not; but native-born, presumptive inheritors of membership must ‘disclaim’ their inheritance and emigrate when they come of age if they wish to avoid the associated burdens. I first review the interpretative challenges of Locke’s treatment of express and tacit consent, then produce the textual evidence in favour of a view that combines express consent and inheritance. Finally, I clarify gaps and puzzles in Locke’s text by comparing it to the legal context in which he is writing. The article seeks to explain Locke’s hopes for the inter-generational stability of voluntary society.
10.53765/20512988.46.4.604.title: ‘No Small Tye’: Locke on Inter-Generational Allegiance

10.53765/20512988.46.4.634.abstract: This article traces Montesquieu’s thoughts on legislative education, the foremost subject in The Spirit of the Laws . Returning to his unfinished, final mature work, the Essay on Taste , it follows the relationship between reason and art as Montesquieu theorizes and practices it; doing so, the article examines, in a new light, three related, difficult subjects: the forms of legislation; the mysterious summit of the Laws , Book XXIX; and the author’s ambivalent relationship to Plato.
10.53765/20512988.46.4.634.title: The Spirit of the Legislator: Art and Education in Montesquieu

10.53765/20512988.46.4.663.abstract: Self-deception is a problem of overriding significance, and Jean-Jacques Rousseau’s treatment of this problem is widely recognized to be among the most sophisticated of his era. Yet virtually no attention has been paid to the analysis of self-deception in a work Rousseau himself called the best and most useful’ of the eighteenth century – The Profession of Faith of the Savoyard Vicar . In this article I reconstruct that analysis, arguing that the Vicar himself is engaged in an intentional effort to acquire and maintain false beliefs. If successful, this argument not only turns conventional readings of The Profession – which emphasize the Vicar’s sincere love of truth – on their collective head but also promises to enrich contemporary philosophical and social scientific conversations about self-deception.
10.53765/20512988.46.4.663.title: He Can’t Handle the Truth: Self-Deception in The Profession of Faith of the Savoyard Vicar

10.53765/20512988.46.4.683.abstract: In 1785, Noah Webster was writing the schoolbooks that made him America’s most influential educator. The same year, he published two ‘fan fiction’ sequels to Rousseau’s Emile: or On Education and he tried to replicate the civic-education journey described in book five of Emile . Webster’s focus on book five, and on imagining what comes after it, indicates that he considered the education in Emile’s earlier books a fait accompli . What America still required to achieve nationhood was Rousseau’s fused project of female education and (male) civic education. America had its ‘Emiles’. Now, to complete its education, it needed Sophie’.
10.53765/20512988.46.4.683.title: Emiles and Sophies: How Noah Webster Educated America’s Youth Like Characters from Rousseau

10.53765/20512988.46.4.713.abstract: Most accounts of Tocqueville emphasize his analysis of liberty and equality, but far less attention has been given to his treatment of dignity ( dignité ). Whereas aristocratic societies organized conduct around the comparative logic of honour, Tocqueville recognized that democratic societies required a different moral foundation that would preserve the worth of individuals without relying on rank. This article argues that Tocqueville’s reflections on dégradation – the erosion of status, self-respect and mutual obligation – reveal an underlying preoccupation with sustaining dignity as the moral substrate of democratic life. Drawing on Democracy in America , The Old Regime and the Revolution , Memoir on Pauperism and Tocqueville’s correspondence, I show that his concern with dignity clarifies both his critique of the manufacturing aristocracy and his defence of religion, associations, local institutions and public opinion. By reconstructing Tocqueville’s implicit theory of dignity, the article demonstrates that dignity is not ancillary but essential to the preservation of liberty and equality in modern democracy.
10.53765/20512988.46.4.713.title: ‘An Enthusiasm for Liberty and for the Dignity of the Human Race’: Honour, Dignity and Degradation in Tocqueville’s Thought

10.53765/20512988.46.4.736.abstract: Thomas Carlyle’s political thought regarding Russia has been almost entirely ignored. Carlyle’s interest in Russia burst forth suddenly in 1842, being expressed in Past and Present (1843). Following the 1848 Revolutions, there was a resurgence in Russophobia throughout Europe, which Carlyle sought to controvert in Latter-Day Pamphlets (1850). During the Crimean War (1853‐6), Carlyle continued to praise Russia and denigrated the British war effort, leading the press to chastize him for his lack of patriotism. Undeterred, Carlyle’s Frederick the Great (1858‐65) panegyrized the Russian nation and its czars, particularly at the expense of the Poles. The culmination of Carlyle’s public engagement for Russia came during the Great Eastern Crisis of 1875‐8. Throughout, Carlyle perpetuated the eighteenth-century enlightenment narrative of Russia as a ‘civilizing’ imperial power.
10.53765/20512988.46.4.736.title: The Hero as Czar: Thomas Carlyle and Political Russophilia

10.53765/20512988.46.4.764.abstract: The English pluralists believed that institutions of higher education were paradigmatic examples of group-life – purposeful associations that, in their fellowship, denied the absolute sovereignty of the state. This article addresses the absence of sustained study of the university as an object of pluralist theorizing by four important pluralists: J.N. Figgis, G.D.H. Cole, Harold Laski and Ernest Barker. They defended the academic freedom of the institution against perceived threats from both the state and organized interests. Despite their differences, and sometimes radical views, their account of the ideal life of the university relied on a conception of public interest that took cues from the church, the trades union and even the state itself, and identified a position that was neither institutionally secular nor rigidly neutral.
10.53765/20512988.46.4.764.title: Don Liberty: English Pluralists on the Modern University

10.53765/20512988.47.1.1.abstract: ‘Kings are called gods by the prophetical King David because they sit upon God his throne in the earth and have the count of their administration to give unto him.’ So wrote James I in his True Lawe of Free Monarchies (1598), here making use of a notion with deep roots in the medieval past that referring to a king as a ‘god’ (as is arguably done in Psalm 81) might under some circumstances be permissible. The present article considers responses to the rhetorical deification of kings and other powerful men in writings attributed to King Alfred the Great: principally those of his lawbook, but also unrecognized instances in his translations of Gregory the Great, Boëthius and Augustine. All show Alfred to resist such language, perhaps because he found it inherently distasteful, but more likely because it was in his own time applied more often to bishops than kings. Defending the privileges of the episcopate often involved quoting the apocryphal legend of Constantine’s address to his bishops: ‘You are gods, so established by the true God; go forth, and consider among yourselves your disputes, for it is not fitting that we judge gods ( Vos dii estis , a vero Deo constituti : ite , et inter vos causas vestras discutite , quia dignum non est ut nos judicemus deos ).’ This tradition competed with another that encouraged rulers to cultivate humility; both are manifest in Alfredian writings to an extent as yet unappreciated and afford a sense of his own struggles to devise an appropriate language for power and authority.
10.53765/20512988.47.1.1.title: Diis Non Detrahes : The Biblical ‘Gods’ and Alfredian Notions of Royal Government

10.53765/20512988.47.1.121.abstract: Rousseau’s concept amour-propre has become the subject of renewed debates. Inspired by Nicholas Dent’s reinterpretation of the term, it is now a widespread view that amour-propre is a positive phenomenon in Rousseau’s moral philosophy, a longing for equal recognition rather than an urge to dominate everybody else. The present article challenges this reading. It does so by going back to Dent’s 1988 work on Rousseau to question the textual evidence for his interpretation. It also challenges the compatibility of Dent’s views with Rousseau’s moral psychology in general. Finally, the article offers an alternative solution to the problem of social life in Rousseau’s philosophy.
10.53765/20512988.47.1.121.title: Amour-Propre According to Rousseau: On the Shortcomings of the Prevailing Consensus

10.53765/20512988.47.1.143.abstract: This article proposes a synchronic-diachronic reading of a specific antidemocratic language that shaped the intellectual history of England. It suggests that, from the early seventeenth to the late nineteenth century, an ideologically diverse body of thinkers similarly and consistently criticized democracy not just as a government but as a plebeian way of life dominated by the licentious and cruel multitude-mob-mass — not by the people and not by liberty. It thus presents a significant series of texts that — in reaction to calls for manhood suffrage and for increased political participation expressed around the times of the 1640s Civil Wars, the internationally revolutionary 1780s–90s and the reform acts concerning the extension of the franchise (1832, 1867, 1884) — attacked democracy for its devastating consequences on politics, morality and civilization. These texts aimed to prove that vicious individuals wanted ‘extreme’ democracy so as to give their vices free rein, while, in turn, encouraging a morally wicked disposition among the lower orders (‘doing as one likes’).
10.53765/20512988.47.1.143.title: The Foundations of English Anti-Democratic Thought c.1630s–1880s: Historiography, Method and History

10.53765/20512988.47.1.37.abstract: This article examines three contributions offered by John of Paris, Giles of Rome and James of Viterbo in the wake of a famous contest between Boniface VIII and Philip IV. Each takes up the Aristotelian principle that what is posterior in time is more perfect than what is prior , which leads to a consideration of the nature, origin and scope of the ‘two powers’, the potestas spiritualis and the potestas temporalis . Their reflections demonstrate medieval efforts to harmonize historical contentions regarding the efficient or agential causes of power, with more abstract or formal considerations of dignity, legitimacy and hierarchy.
10.53765/20512988.47.1.37.title: History, Hierarchy and the ‘Powers that Be’ in Medieval Political Thought

10.53765/20512988.47.1.66.abstract: While recent studies have revisited Giovanni Botero’s notion of monarchy, his ideas on democracies and aristocracies remain largely unexplored. Rather than presenting his preference for monarchy as a fixed teleological commitment, this article explores Botero’s comparative reflections on republics — popular and aristocratic — to reveal a more nuanced conception of political order than is typically attributed to him. Botero’s ideas are situated within his intellectual milieu and juxtaposed with those of his contemporaries and intellectual adversaries, including, but not limited to, Jean Bodin and Niccolò Machiavelli.
10.53765/20512988.47.1.66.title: Between Monarchy and Republicanism: Aristocracies and Democracies in Giovanni Botero’s Political Thought

10.53765/20512988.47.1.96.abstract: This article examines Johannes Althusius’ engagement in his Politica with the theories of public power prevailing in his time, particularly the theories put forward by Jean Bodin and other supporters of absolute sovereignty. Althusius has often been interpreted as responding primarily to the claims of these writers about the location of sovereign power. The principal thesis of the present article, however, is that Althusius is engaging no less critically with a number of associated arguments about the nature of lawful power, especially the views on the basis of which Bodin and his followers had erected their defence of absolute sovereignty.
10.53765/20512988.47.1.96.title: Johannes Althusius and the Rejection of Absolutism

10.53765/20512988.47.2.181.abstract: In the Melian Dialogue, Thucydides’ Athenians famously assert that justice is only relevant among those subject to ‘equal necessity’ ( apo tēs isēs anankēs ). But what exactly does this mean? Interpreters have long assumed it to be a statement of power’s priority over ethics, thus identifying the Athenians as prototypical political realists. In this article, however, I challenge this reading, as well as the ‘degenerative’ interpretation of the Athenian mindset built upon it. I argue that both are out of tune with Thucydides’ ‘interpretivist’ understanding of necessity ( anankē ) and the Melian Dialogue’s intertextual engagement with Greek epic. Together, these aspects of Thucydides’ political thought point towards a more critical exploration of the tensions internal to the position of the Melian oligarchs, who are both ‘strong’ within the city of Melos and ‘weak’ in the face of the Athenian threat. The result is a richer account of how subjective forces interact with objective circumstances to result in intractable conflict and tragic violence.
10.53765/20512988.47.2.181.title: Compelling Justice: Translating Necessity in Thucydides’ Melian Dialogue

10.53765/20512988.47.2.212.abstract: Aristotle is widely identified as foundational to the understanding of tyranny as a form of political enslavement, wherein the ruled are treated ‘like a slave’ insofar as they are subjected to the arbitrary will of another. This article challenges the collapse of Aristotelian tyranny into arbitrary rule by reconstructing what it means, on Aristotle’s understanding, for tyrants to rule ‘like a master’. Aristotle suggests that tyrants and slave masters are akin insofar as they are often driven by a longing for supremacy , a structurally embedded desire to secure a legible position of preeminent standing. The recognition of such supremacy is important for despots because it promises to vouchsafe their security from those whom they oppress. But Aristotle suggests that such desired standing is often internally unstable; oppressed actors like slaves and tyrannized citizens harbour a sense of worth or merit ( axia ) that is incompatible with the despotism of slavery or tyranny, and the repressive means through which despotic actors attempt to diminish expressions of axia among the oppressed can prove self-defeating. This article demonstrates that Aristotle’s insights into the psychological and structural dynamics that attend this longing for supremacy inform his treatments of slave systems found in Sparta, Thessaly and Crete, his insights into political repression under tyrannies, as well as other relationships characterized by asymmetrical power and unwilling subjection discussed throughout the Politics .
10.53765/20512988.47.2.212.title: ‘Like a Master:’ Aristotle on Tyranny, Slavery and the Longing for Supremacy

10.53765/20512988.47.2.241.abstract: Drawing on a comprehensive study of the ‘by nature’ (φv´σει) formulation across the extant Aristotelean corpus in light of the linguistic construction of ‘ slave by nature ’ (φv´σει δOũλς) in Politics I , this article thematizes two separate senses of ‘nature’ (φv´σις) embedded in Aristotle’s general theory of nature-based enslavement: dispositional and categorical. Whereas a dispositional account highlights the sociostructural nature ofslavery, a categorical perspective emphasizes an enslaved person’s pre-habituated traits or natural essence as passed down congenitally and climatologically. These two perspectives end up being co-constitutive in Aristotle’s justification of enslavement. Far from being an internal critique seeking to mitigate the many harms of slavery, Aristotle’s theory thus has the effect of supporting the continuous political reproduction and legitimation of the institution of slavery.
10.53765/20512988.47.2.241.title: Slavery by Disposition and by Categoricity: Revisiting Politics and Nature in Aristotle’s Nature-Based Justifications of Enslavement

10.53765/20512988.47.2.270.abstract: Scholarship on the political thought of Marsilius of Padua has long oscillated between portraying him as a covert democrat or an advocate of aristocratic rule. These competing interpretations hinge on differing claims about his influences, whether derived from the Aristotelianism of Moerbeke’s translation of the Politics or from the civic practices of the Italian comuni . While these perspectivesremain central, scholars have overlooked another crucial context: the corporatism of the University of Paris. This paper enriches existing interpretations of Marsilius’ political theory by arguing for a complementary influence of the university’s institutional structures on his conception of political order.
10.53765/20512988.47.2.270.title: Marsilius’ Defensor Pacis and the University of Paris

10.53765/20512988.47.2.295.abstract: Building on the political philosophy of Aristotle and Cicero, civil philosophers in the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries believed that the commonwealth could neither come into existence, nor subsist, without commerce. This article explores this belief, with a focus on French and English thought. In order to do this, it recovers the iridescent meanings of ‘commerce’ in later civil philosophy, including its related terms ‘company’, ‘communication’, ‘society’, ‘conversation’ and ‘trade’. In contrast to its more restricted modern meaning, commerce in early modern thought denoted the complex web of human relations and exchange that led to the formation of communities, from the family and friendship, to trading companies and the commonwealth itself.
10.53765/20512988.47.2.295.title: ‘Commerce’ and ‘Commonwealth’ in France and England, 1550-1615

10.53765/20512988.47.2.326.abstract: Examination of Montesquieu’s treatment of legislators in his Spirit of the Laws provides a new perspective on the scholarly debate as to whether Montesquieu approaches the global diversity he documents there with the attitude of a particularist or of a universalist. As he reveals that previous philosophic writers have served as legislators, so he himself becomes one; Montesquieu offers, in Book 12, a table of laws and corresponding punishments. This is his own legislative act, as it prescribes and does not describe. His legislation is, he declares, according to nature. It is applicable everywhere once peoples’ spirits are prepared for it.
10.53765/20512988.47.2.326.title: Montesquieu on Legislators and as a Legislator: a Reconsideration of his Particularism and Universalism

10.53765/20512988.47.2.349.abstract: This article argues that while the instability and violence of the French Revolution has been overwhelmingly attributed to the transfer of unitary sovereignty from king to people, popular sovereignty was neither conceptually novel nor inherently destabilizing in 1789. We begin by drawing on early modern political theory, most importantly Bodin, d’Argenson and Rousseau, to argue that democracy was understood to be as much a form of government as a type of sovereignty. By tracing successive experiments from mixed government in 1789 to ‘revolutionary government’ in 1794 to imperial government under Napoleon, the article shows how suspicion towards government shaped revolutionary politics and drove institutional change. The Terror and the First Empire emerge not as inevitable outcomes of democracy, characterized by unitary popular sovereignty, but as contingent responses to perceived failures of previous governmental arrangements. By recovering a neglected history of democracy, this article renews the ambition of providing a political matrix for situating revolutionary politics within the longer historical arc of modern democratic politics.
10.53765/20512988.47.2.349.title: Sovereignty and Government in the French Revolution
