10.5840/philtoday2018215199.abstract: Rebecca Tuvel’s controversial “In Defense of Transracialism” has been criticized for a lack of engagement with critical race theory. Disengagement with salient material on race is a consistent feature of the philosophical conversation out of which it arises. In this article, I trace the origins of feminist philosophy’s disengaged and distorted view of “transracialism” and racial passing through the work of Janice Raymond, Christine Overall, and Cressida Heyes, and consider some of the relevant work on passing that is omitted in the philosophy of “transracialism.” Finally, I offer methodological suggestions to avoid such distortions and omissions in feminist philosophy.
10.5840/philtoday2018215199.title: (Dis)Engaging with Race Theory: Feminist Philosophy’s Debate on “Transracialism” as a Case Study

10.5840/philtoday2018223200.abstract: In this essay, I reply to critiques of my article “In Defense of Transracialism.” Echoing Chloë Taylor and Lewis Gordon’s remarks on the controversy over my article, I first reflect on the lack of intellectual generosity displayed in response to my paper. In reply to Kris Sealey, I next argue that it is dangerous to hinge the moral acceptability of a particular identity or practice on what she calls a collective co-signing. In reply to Sabrina Hom, I suggest that relying on the language of passing to describe transracialism is potentially misleading. In reply to Tina Botts, I both defend analytic philosophy of race against her multiple criticisms and suggest that Botts’s remarks risk complicity with a form of transphobia that Talia Mae Bettcher calls the Basic Denial of Authenticity. I end by gesturing toward a more inclusive understanding of racial identity.
10.5840/philtoday2018223200.title: Racial Transitions and Controversial Positions: Reply to Taylor, Gordon, Sealey, Hom, and Botts

10.5840/philtoday2018227202.abstract: Examining the ways in which two representatives of the “theological turn in French phenomenology” speak of the interrelationship between philosophy and theology, one may detect a number of tendencies which are deleterious both to philosophy and theology. The idea of an autonomous philosophy, pursued as an end in itself, needs to be defended against claims that philosophy can only flourish under theological tutelage. Again, the integrity of theology as a science of faith excludes any identification of theology as a kind of philosophy. Interaction between the two disciplines, especially in the border areas of apologetics, fundamental theology, religious philosophy, and philosophy of religion, can be fruitful only if a keen sense of their radical difference of orientation is sustained. Behind the swamping of phenomenology by theological concerns lies a series of misunderstandings of metaphysics and its overcoming as well as a misguided notion that phenomenology allows revealed theology to re-enter the French university under the rubric of philosophy.
10.5840/philtoday2018227202.title: Phenomenology and Theology: Respecting the Boundaries

10.5840/philtoday201828195.title: Race and Method: The Tuvel Affair

10.5840/philtoday201829197.abstract: My reading of Tuvel’s defense of transracialism focuses on her critiques of three main objections to a transracial identity. Tuvel attempts to show how her defense of transracialism stands in the face of these objections. However, I argue that her position is not sufficiently immune to them. In other words, my response delineates the ways in which all three objections remain, and effectively undermine her argument in favor of transracial identities. Additionally, through the question of white allyship, I ask about the moral and political consequences of choosing to identify as transracial. I show that, without a clear account of what an existential choice of racial transitioning implies for allyship across race, Tuvel does not sufficiently establish the differences between the historical constitutions of racialized and sexualized identities. In failing to engage with these moral/political implications, Tuvel’s position does not address the complex relationship between individual agency and collective accountability.
10.5840/philtoday201829197.title: Transracialism and White Allyship: A Response to Rebecca Tuvel

10.5840/philtoday2018611221.abstract: Rhetoric concerns how in speech human beings open up a place for civil possibility, a place where, as a community of speakers and hearers, they engage with questions of how best to conceive and respond to challenges arising out of the world that they share. In rhetoric the community of speakers and hearers is not only called into being but so too the nature of the topos or place that is shared, a determination that is timely or historical. The recent publication of Heidegger’s 1924 lectures on Aristotle’s Rhetoric explores this idea of rhetoric. These lectures raise questions for how and whether Heidegger sustained this conception in his later work, and also questions for how this conception may have influenced Arendt’s approach to political thought. Arendt’s conception of the role of the spectator who engages in the activity of understanding in order to “try to be at home in the world” is especially pertinent here. Arendt’s writing, so far as it calls into being a rhetorical relationship between her “speech” and her hearers/readers, is best appreciated as rhetoric.
10.5840/philtoday2018611221.title: Arendt and Rhetoric

10.5840/philtoday2018622231.title: Patrick Hayes and Jan Wilm, eds., Beyond the Ancient Quarrel: Literature, Philosophy, and J. M. Coetzee

10.5840/philtoday2018624249.title: The Practice of Philosophy: Truth-Telling, Vulnerability, and Risk

10.5840/philtoday20191030283.abstract: We propose to approach Simondon’s writing as a techno-aesthetic object, as a singular prose of thought. To do so requires assuming Simondon’s technological proposal as the creation of a new mode of knowledge about the technicality of objects, abandoning the idea that the word “technology” can serve to designate a given state of things. This proposal, cultural and educational at the same time, requires a new way of approaching the world, starting with the way we approach reading. The techno-aesthetics of Simondon’s writing also requires a techno-aesthetic reading.
10.5840/philtoday20191030283.title: The Birth of Techno-Logos: The Writing of Simondon as a Techno-Aesthetic Object

10.5840/philtoday20191111293.abstract: Unlike the free interpretations of Simondon’s genetic encyclopaedism, the constraining exegesis of this doctrine resolves the paradoxes that are essential for it to be constructed in its depth and subtlety. Now, at the root of these simple paradoxes lies what is no longer one, but which constitutes a true contradiction, of a methodological type. That is why today we need an encompassing refounding of Simondon’s genetic ontology, which makes it possible to eliminate the contradiction by transforming this ontology into a translation of a new first problematic, called “archi-reflexive semantics.” Such is the program of the global but radically antidogmatic system of the individuation of (making-)sense, or “human ecology”, the ultimate telos of which is political-economic and articulates itself with a decentered humanism refounding the law outside ethics.
10.5840/philtoday20191111293.title: From Genetic Encyclopaedism to Human Ecology

10.5840/philtoday2019111288.abstract: The article develops the different meanings of the Simondonian idea of the transindividual, reconstructs the different interpretations that have been made about it, and considers its potentiality to think contemporary phenomena. For this, first, it points out the uses of the term transindividual before Simondon’s conceptualization of it. Second, it analyzes the definitions of the concept that appear in his doctoral theses of 1958 and distinguishes his different senses (ontogenetic, metaphysical, ethical, technical, etc.). Third, it reconstructs the contemporary debate about the transindividual and defines three moments (1989-1998, 1999-2005, and 2005-2015). Finally, it concludes by reflecting on the philosophical and epistemological potentiality of the idea of the transindividual to think about complex processes marked by the association of technological, psychosocial, and ethical-political dimensions.
10.5840/philtoday2019111288.title: Through and Beyond the Transindividual

10.5840/philtoday20191218294.abstract: This essay considers the phenomenon of almanacs, encyclopedias, glossaries, lexicons, word books, vocabularies, companions, and (theoretical) toolboxes, which appears to be an outstanding feature of humanities today. By limiting her discussion to six specific examples of this genre, the author asks the following questions: Why is it that this method became so prolific? What are the objectives of almanacs, glossaries, and vocabularies? What do they do to thinking, writing, researching? What can they say about the moment we are in? And how do they contribute to defining this moment? Those questions orient discussions around humanities today toward the ethico-political practice of thinking otherwise.
10.5840/philtoday20191218294.title: Think We Must! (Otherwise)

10.5840/philtoday20191220295.abstract: The central argument in this essay is that while the concept of entanglement offers materialism the promise of a conceptually rich field of new “entangled” entities, by itself, entanglement is ill-equipped to contend with the thorny questions of how power is organized among those entities. This essay proposes that decoherence provides a welcome complement to entanglement.
10.5840/philtoday20191220295.title: Quantum Decoherence

10.5840/philtoday2019611258.abstract: The present study is an attempt to contribute to the debates on the relationship between spiritual traditions and Descartes’s Meditations. Taking its point of departure from Pierre Hadot’s inspiring studies, the article aims to describe the nature of the philosophical practice that Meditations embodies and to discuss the ways in which the work can be located in the history of the relations between theory and practice. To this end, Hadot’s suggestion that Meditations should be read as a set of spiritual exercises will be criticized through an analysis of the nature of the “non-argumentative” or “experiential” level that is at work in Descartes’s text. By showing that the transformation intended by Descartes does not reach beyond the level of cognition, it will be argued that even though Descartes makes use of certain key elements of the spiritualist literature, he belongs to the modern age of “philosophy without spirituality.”
10.5840/philtoday2019611258.title: Descartes and Spiritual Exercises: A Critique of Pierre Hadot's Historical Narrative

10.5840/philtoday2019827279.abstract: Much French philosophy of the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries has been marked by the positive valorization of alterity, an ethical position that has recently received a vigorous assault from Alain Badiou’s privilege of sameness. This article argues that Badiou shares a great deal in common with the philosophies of alterity from which he seeks to distance himself, and that Michel Serres’s little-known account of alterity offers a much more radical alternative to the ethics of difference. Drawing on both translated and as yet untranslated works, I argue that the Serresian ontology of inclination, along with his conceptual personae of the hermaphrodite and the parasite, informs ethical and political positions that offer a distinctive ethics and politics that present fresh insights about the relation between the singular and the universal, the contingency of market exchange, and the nature of violence.
10.5840/philtoday2019827279.title: Not More of the Same: Michel Serres’s Challenge to the Ethics of Alterity

10.5840/philtoday2019827280.abstract: This paper attempts to situate Derrida’s newly discovered Geschlecht III in the four-part series Derrida dedicated to the question of sexual difference in Heidegger. Taking its point of departure from an interview conducted two years prior to Geschlecht I, the paper retraces Derrida’s itinerary toward the culminating point of the Geschlecht series, Geschlecht III, the “magnet” that orients and attracts the other three. I argue that Derrida’s initial enthusiasm for a Heideggerian “pre-dual sexuality” in Geschlecht I is significantly tempered by Derrida’s meticulous reading of Heidegger in Geschlecht III, where his reservations vis-à-vis Heidegger’s neutralization of sexual difference become all the more serious and explicit. As I show, Derrida’s “dream” of a “doubly asymmetrical” sexual relation to the other remains incompatible with the sexual gentleness Heidegger imagines between brother and sister, an ultimately Christian incest that will yet again threaten to neutralize and erase the more radical sexual difference Derrida is trying to think.
10.5840/philtoday2019827280.title: From Neutral Dasein to a Gentle Twofold: Sexual Difference in Heidegger and Derrida

10.5840/philtoday201985272.abstract: This essay explores Jean-Luc Nancy’s philosophical return to Cartesian philosophy, specifically to Descartes’s preoccupation with the relation of mind and body, as a fertile ground from which to develop an ontology of the body in (1992). It explores Nancy’s reasons for revisiting the Cartesian thinking framework, which on the face of it, is of little value to an ontology of the body. I argue that Descartes’s impasse in accounting for both mind/body dualism and their union constitutes Nancy’s point of departure in constructing an ontology of the body in , thereby transforming Descartes’s impasse into a productive aporia, in the Derridean sense of the term. To fully understand the significance of the notion of “relation” in Nancy’s’ philosophy, I turn to his reading of Lacan’s famous aphorism “there is no sexual relation” and explore its ontological implications.
10.5840/philtoday201985272.title: Jean-Luc Nancy and the Extension of the Mind

10.5840/philtoday2020108357.abstract: This essay contends that Stanley Cavell’s criterion of “good enough justice,” which designates the minimal condition of social justice necessary for his perfectionist understanding of ethical selfhood, constitutes an avoidance—rather than an acknowledgment—of the problem of injustice. Taking Cavell’s misreading of Walter Benjamin as exemplary of this tendency, the essay shows how Cavell’s moral perfectionism consistently converts questions about the suffering of others into a problem of the self and its conscience, thereby avoiding the ethical claim at the heart of Benjamin’s project.
10.5840/philtoday2020108357.title: Good Enough Justice?: Stanley Cavell and Walter Benjamin on the Moral Demands of Justice

10.5840/philtoday20201110368.abstract: This essay considers the pandemic as a consequence of the planetary condition. It goes on to ask: Can philosophy contribute to the elucidation of the planetary, or is philosophy, in the words of Heidegger, already completed in and as the planetary? What kind of relation to the planetary will it desire to have?
10.5840/philtoday20201110368.title: Philosophy and the Planetary

10.5840/philtoday2020128312.abstract: Ruinology is defined here as the study of the speculative reconstruction of ruins. Its remit encompasses both the study of the mechanisms of ruination as well as attempts to reverse-engineer ruination and reconstruct architectural remains.
10.5840/philtoday2020128312.title: Ruinology

10.5840/philtoday2020128318.abstract: Transversal Posthumanities emerge within the posthuman convergence of posthumanism and postanthropocentrism. Environmental, medical, and digital humanities reposition academic practice towards advanced technologies and climate change issues. A neomaterialist theoretical framework will help distinguish different kinds of Posthumanities: from the profit-oriented knowledge production practices of cognitive capitalism, to community-driven, non-profit experiments with minor knowledges.
10.5840/philtoday2020128318.title: Transversal Posthumanities

10.5840/philtoday202013296.abstract: This text elaborates an understanding of abstraction as fundamental to how we think from a closer look at relationships between abstraction, movement, materiality and lived experience. Starting from Whitehead-inspired reflections on ab­straction by Alberto Toscano and Brian Massumi, the differences between their respective readings of his work are shown to be indicative for their different conceptions of the relationships between abstraction, the concrete, and lived experience. The text then continues to elaborate how Alva Noë’s enactive approach to perception illumi­nates the central role of movement and sensorimotor skills in the emergence of abstractions from the continuity of process that is reality, and could contribute to further understanding of the relationship between movement and abstraction as what Massumi describes as the incorporeal dimension of the real. Finally, this text reflects on the potential of movement practices (including dance) and technology to become part of how abstraction is achieved.
10.5840/philtoday202013296.title: Abstraction

10.5840/philtoday202019301.abstract: This essay argues for a transversal posthumanities-based pedagogy, rooted in an attentive ethico-onto-epistemology, by reading the schizoanalytical praxes of Deleuzoguattarian theory alongside the work of various feminist new materialist scholars.
10.5840/philtoday202019301.title: Ethico-onto-epistemology

10.5840/philtoday202062342.abstract: At an important moment in his reading of Heidegger in Geschlecht III, Derrida wields a pair of semi-technical terms (“polysemia” and “dissemination”) from his own earlier work, and uses them to identify a classical, indeed Aristotelian, vein in Heidegger’s reading of Trakl. This gesture is complex, both in that, in spite of appearances, the Mehrdeutigkeit Heidegger identifies in Trakl is not essentially to do with the term Geschlecht, and in that Derrida’s presentation of Aristotle’s views about polysemia is perhaps over-simplified, or at least leaves open the possibility of a more generous reading. Derrida’s notion of dissemination is shown not to entail a mere exacerbation of polysemia, but a quasi-semantic re-marking of the “syntax” that allows for any semantic effects at all. It is suggested that the fact that this marking can be described by Derrida as “monotonous” might open onto a slightly different reading both of Aristotle’s understanding of pollachos legomenon and pros hen, and Heidegger’s understanding of the Einklang of Trakl’s poetry.
10.5840/philtoday202062342.title: Geschlecht pollachos legetai: Translation, Polysemia, Dissemination

10.5840/philtoday2021105427.abstract: How should African philosophy be done in African Language? In response to this question, I engage Ngugi and Wiredu in their response to this language question in African philosophy. My aim is to appraise and extend their arguments by answering the question of “how” doing African philosophy in African language can be practically achieved. In this regard, I make a case for the creation of an indigenous cultural language that serves as a means of articulating, communicating and disseminating African philosophical ideas. I suggest the need for African scholars to develop a language culture under the auspices of African Language Network (A.L.N.) that will enable them to do philosophy and present it in an African language. I show that African philosophy done in a foreign or colonial language is like dressing Africa in a borrowed rope, and that as long as African scholars continue to overlook this, the lofty goal of restoring the lost glory of Africa, the gains and further progress in African philosophy, rather than being consolidated, may become greatly hampered. Recognizing the diversity of languages in African culture, I present Afrolingualism as the key to achieving this end. Afrolingualism is a conscientious effort by African scholars to contrive a unanimously accepted indigenous language of discourse in philosophy.
10.5840/philtoday2021105427.title: On “How” to Do African Philosophy in African Language: Some Objections and Extensions

10.5840/philtoday2021217386.abstract: The past few years have seen a dramatic backlash against identity politics from academics such as Michael Sandel, Kwame Appiah, Mark Lilla, and Francis Fukuyama. In the vocabulary of identity conceptions, we can classify this as a reaction to a growing dissatisfaction with the perceived hollowness and ineffectiveness of “authenticity” that calls for a return to “sincerity”—or a “Political New Sincerity.” We argue that a third identity paradigm is in play as well, namely “profilicity.” This profile-based approach to understanding oneself, others, and the world has had a major impact on social and political life, and yet has gone largely unnoticed or otherwise been mis-diagnosed. Our analysis provides a critical reflection on the emergence of profilicity to pave the way for developing insights into our changing sociopolitical and inter-personal landscapes.
10.5840/philtoday2021217386.title: Political New Sincerity and Profilicity: On the Decline of Identity Politics and Authenticity

10.5840/philtoday2021412394.abstract: In this dialogue with Yuk Hui, Eduardo Viveiros de Castro discusses his work on the Amerindian perspectivism, multinaturalism; the relation between nature, culture and technics in his ethnographic studies; as well as the necessity of a non-anthropocentric definition of technology. He also discusses a haunting futurism of ecological crisis and automation of the Anthropocene, and explores a “strategic primitivism” as survival tool.
10.5840/philtoday2021412394.title: For a Strategic Primitivism: A Dialogue between Eduardo Viveiros de Castro and Yuk Hui

10.5840/philtoday2021414397.abstract: Ours is an age of general automation. The factory that produced proletarians now extends to the biosphere; consequently, disautomatization is needed, which is the real meaning of autonomy. Autonomy and automatism must be reconceived as a composition rather than an opposition. Knowledge depends on hypomnesic automatisms that open up the possibility of what Socrates called “thinking for oneself”; digitalization thus requires a new epistemology that entails questions of political and libidinal economy. Today, automatization serves the autonomization of technics more than noetic autonomy, but reconceiving the latter necessarily involves reconsidering the meaning and character of desire. Greta Thunberg’s diagnosis of the irresponsibility of the generation before hers exposes the fact that the knowledge necessary to combat the consequences of contemporary technological development has been destroyed. The only possible counter to this irresponsibility lies in the reconstitution of knowledge, understood as the means by which humans struggle against entropy and anthropy.
10.5840/philtoday2021414397.title: Elements for a Neganthropology of Automatic Man

10.5840/philtoday2021519407.abstract: Across the world, militaries are racing to acquire and develop new capabilities based on the latest in machine learning, neural networks, and artificial intelligence (AI). In this paper, I argue that the shift into military AI is shaping human behaviour in heretofore unacknowledged and morally significant ways. Following Anders, I argue that as the human becomes digitally co-machinistic (mitmaschinell), they are compelled to adopt a logic of speed and optimisation in their ethical reasoning. The consequence of this is a form a moral de-skilling, whereby military personnel working with digital infrastructures and interfaces become less able to act and decide as moral agents. This is an especially concerning development when it comes to the conduct of war, where the moral stakes could not be higher.
10.5840/philtoday2021519407.title: Silicon Valley Goes to War: Artificial Intelligence, Weapons Systems, and Moral Agency

10.5840/philtoday2021519408.abstract: This paper examines the development and technological mediation of the concept of solidarity. We focus on the workplace as a focal point of solidarity relations, and utilise a phenomenological approach to describe and analyse those relations. Workplace solidarity, which has been historically concretised through social objects such as labor unions, is of particular political relevance since it has played an outsize role in the broader struggle for social, economic, and political rights, recognition, and equality. We argue that the use of automated decision support systems (ADS) in labor process management may negatively affect the formation of these relations. As solidarity motivates collective political action and risk-taking, the mediation and potential obstruction of solidarity relations by ADS is politically significant. We contribute to the growing literature on the “future of work” problem in elucidating the technological mediation of workplace solidarity.
10.5840/philtoday2021519408.title: The Algorithmic Disruption of Workplace Solidarity: Phenomenology and the Future of Work Question

10.5840/philtoday2021524415.abstract: Jean-Paul Sartre’s theory of “the look” has generally been understood as an argument for the impossibility of mutual recognition between consciousnesses. Being-looked-at reveals me as an object for the other, but I can never grasp this object that I am. I argue here that the chapter “The Look” in Being and Nothingness has been widely misunderstood, causing many to dismiss Sartre’s view unfairly. Like Hegel’s account of recognition, Sartre’s “look” is meant as a theory of successful mutual recognition that proves the existence of others. Yet Sartre claims that such an account is plausible only if recognition is affective, not cognitive. Situating Sartre’s account of the look within his technical understanding of affect’s distinctness from cognition not only enables a better understanding of Sartre’s view, but also reveals a compelling alternative to the understanding of self-other relations in contemporary affect theory.
10.5840/philtoday2021524415.title: Sartre’s Affective Turn: Shame as Recognition in “The Look”

10.5840/philtoday2022318445.abstract: This article challenges the recurrent critique that Pierre Hadot’s identification of ancient philosophy with the practice of spiritual exercises introduces a non- or irrational dimension into metaphilosophy. The occasion to do this is provided by Kerem Eksen’s recent reading of Descartes’s Meditations as consisting of solely intellectual, rather than spiritual, exercises—since the latter, Eksen claims, involve extrarational means and ends. Part 2 presents an alternative account of the role of cognition in the ancient meditatio at issue in understanding Descartes’s antecedents. This account is indebted to Michel Foucault’s characterization of ancient meditation as involving two cognitive mechanisms: an appropriation of thought, and an experiment in identification. Part 3 argues that attempts such as Eksen’s to depict spiritual exercises as wholly noncognitive themselves are the product of an “unexamined Cartesianism” that is fundamentally at odds with the monistic psychology of ancient Stoics like Marcus Aurelius as discussed in Hadot’s studies.
10.5840/philtoday2022318445.title: Of Cartesianism and Spiritual Exercises: Reading Descartes through Hadot, and Hadot through Descartes

10.5840/philtoday2022623456.abstract: Much has been made of the so-called “empirical turn” of “speculative materialism” with thinkers like Quentin Meillassoux championing the material sciences as a new route to absolute reality. According to Meillassoux, the material sciences “provide philosophers access once again to the great outdoors, the absolute outside,” of reality in-itself. One might expect from such encomia the attempt to engage with the products of contemporary science in order to develop a new metaphysics; but, Meillassoux spends almost no time in this way, focusing instead on the form and methods of the material sciences over their actual accomplishments. As a result, his praise rings hollow and his metaphysics remains undeveloped. This paper examines what would happen if we were to take seriously his claims that a new metaphysics be developed from a scientific accounting of material reality by surveying the conclusions of contemporary physics. The paper ends by contrasting such a new speculative and materialistic metaphysics with the speculative nihilism of Ray Brassier.
10.5840/philtoday2022623456.title: The Metaphysics of Speculative Materialism: Reckoning with the Fact of Entropy

10.5840/philtoday202271461.abstract: In his 2018 essay Down to Earth, the French philosopher Bruno Latour proposes a hypothesis that connects a number of contemporary issues, ranging from climate denialism to deregulation and growing inequality. While his hypothesis, namely that the elites act as if they live in another world and are leaving the rest of the world behind, might seem like a conspiracy theory, I will argue that there is a way to make sense of it. To do so, I will turn to two other authors, Timothy Mitchell and Shoshana Zuboff, to highlight the kind of logic that Latour seems to have in mind. In the final section, I will propose to capture the commonalities of these authors through the concept of shifting reciprocities and will return to Latour’s political plea to define one’s territories, reinterpreted as reciprocities.
10.5840/philtoday202271461.title: Gatekeepers and Gated Communities: The Role of Technology in Our Shifting Reciprocities

10.5840/philtoday202278462.abstract: In our article, we argue, following Nelson Goodman and Arthur Danto, that in contrast to the essentialist conception of authenticity, it is more fertile to consider authentic patterns not as the inner core of the person, but as a case of metaphorical exemplification. According to our approach, if we accept that authentic style is a metaphorical exemplification, then, based on Richard Rorty’s concepts of language and metaphor, style can be seen as an exaptation or reuse of symbols previously adapted through cultural selection to other specific functions. To support this approach, we proceed as follows. First, using Goodman’s and Danto’s model, we argue that authentic style can best be grasped through metaphorical exemplification. We then show that the metaphorical use of linguistic, pictorial, and other symbols is the result of exaptation. According to our results, the authentic style is the exaptation of symbols previously adapted to culturally selected functions. We then separate authenticity from creativity through the concepts of style and manner—borrowed from Danto—and we point out that whether a particular symbol is authentic or not is not affected by whether creative or mechanical mental processes are responsible for its creation. Finally, we examine the relationship between authenticity and autonomy, and we show that in an environment that promotes autonomous decisions and authentic style, agents that originally generated inauthentic symbols may be able to produce authentic ones.
10.5840/philtoday202278462.title: Le style c'est l'homme même?: Style and Exaptive Authenticity

10.5840/philtoday202327472.abstract: This essay examines the relationship between African American internal colonialism and democracy, highlighting the complexities of democracy that make it both susceptible to oppressive violence at home and abroad, as well as a potential resource for emancipation and equality. I understand “internal colonialism” here to encompass various terms used by African Americans beginning in the 1830s, including semi-colonialism, domestic colonialism, and a nation within a nation. Much political philosophy assumes that society is “nearly just” or “generally just,” or that oppression and injustice are found in societies that we nonetheless deem legitimate. Centering the complexities and possibilities of democracy instead shifts the focus to how democracy is compatible with violence and injustice, as well as their overcoming. Such a focus leads to a consideration of abolition democracy and the question of what the process of overcoming internal colonialism demands.
10.5840/philtoday202327472.title: Internal Colonialism and Democracy

10.5840/philtoday2023523484.abstract: In dialogue with Kristin Ross and Fred Moten, as well as recent theorizations of destituent power, this article aims to trace the practical logic that governs place-based politics in our anarchic epoch, including the construction of collective formations that defend them.
10.5840/philtoday2023523484.title: Exile and Fragmentation: The New Politics of Place

10.5840/philtoday202354481.abstract: John Dewey’s conception of democracy as the political form devoted to the maximum individual self-realization of the citizenry, in the broadest sense of that term, promises to lift democracy above angry populism while avoiding untenable and contentious metaphysical commitments. The idea of self-realization is traditionally tied to a hierarchical and therefore unacceptable model of society. Dewey breaks this tie by stripping the idea of its metaphysical commitments. But Dewey requires supplementation. I argue that Dewey’s own insights can be best kept alive by being read in light of Stanley Cavell’s understanding of Emersonian Perfectionism, in particular the latter’s focus on the failure of the self to realize itself and its ordinary resistance to doing so. Bringing this Romanticism to bear upon Dewey’s ideas would temper them in important ways, preserving and developing what is best in the rich conception of democratic citizenship he has left us.
10.5840/philtoday202354481.title: Dewey, Self-Realization, and Romanticism

10.5840/philtoday2023628489.abstract: In After Finitude, Quentin Meillassoux speculates from the principle of noncontradiction’s a priori enclosure toward a standpoint of absolute contingency. Based on his propositions, I argue that his thinking continues to reproduce a contradiction between the finitude of the subject and the infinitude of the noumenal world. Accordingly, I eschew the principle of noncontradiction in favor of a principle of contradiction derived from Hermann Levin Goldschmidt’s Contradiction Set Free. Goldschmidt formulates contradiction as an Either-And-Or whereby the two contradictory terms share a space between them in which there elapses a continuous process of negotiation. If the relation between finitude and infinitude is an Either-And-Or, then there is an interpenetration between the finite and the infinite, between bounded subject and noumenal world. Goldschmidt’s method reinvigorates the contradiction with which Meillassoux is grappling and introduces a more immanent mode of infinitude that echoes certain Spinozist and pre-Spinozist strains of Jewish thought.
10.5840/philtoday2023628489.title: Clearing Up Correlationism: Goldschmidt, Meillassoux, and the Problem of Finitude

10.5840/philtoday2023629491.abstract: Goldschmidt’s evocation of Leviticus 19:18 in Contradiction Set Free accomplishes heavy lifting within the distinction of the dialogic from the dialectic. Analogized to a necessary recognition of each particular and unique fulfillment of the immediate command to “love your neighbor as yourself,” dialogue is temporalized within an already near, yet not ever complete, messianic infinite. As an ongoing, active and unfinished composition of unique “nows,” dialogue’s structure is likewise epistemically distinct from the structure of dialectical synthesis. How might this distinction’s lens of Leviticus 19:18 illumine opportunities—and obstacles—for “dialogue” between humans and artificial systems? Does examining the specific case of OpenAI’s ChatGPT under the lens of Goldschmidt’s text suggest that certain questions about generative AI learning capacity might actually be questions of time?
10.5840/philtoday2023629491.title: Dialogue Set Free?: Goldschmidt’s Reading of Leviticus 19:18 Encounters ChatGPT

10.5840/philtoday2023714497.abstract: This article reconstructs Slavoj Žižek’s theory of ideology as a form of fetishistic disavowal. By seeking out Žižek’s relevant influences and clarifying them, the article seeks to make the theory of fetishistic disavowal in politics intelligible to a wider audience. Moreover, the article argues that the theory of ideology advanced by Žižek in this period of his work can be understood as a theory of unconscious defense, a fact that raises important questions about the utility of psychoanalysis for political philosophy. The article also considers issues pertaining to political belief, practical irrationality, and real abstraction.
10.5840/philtoday2023714497.title: Žižek’s Politics of Fetishism

10.5840/philtoday2024126519.abstract: This essay reshapes our understanding of the origin and trajectory of the phenomenology of feelings. In contrast to accepted interpretations, I show that Husserl’s 1896 manuscript “Approval, Value, and Evidence”—and not his 1901 Logical Investigations—is the foundation of his subsequent phenomenology of feelings as it is found in Lectures on Ethics and Value Theory, Ideas I, and other manuscripts. This is for two reasons. First, in the 1896 manuscript—published in Studies Concerning the Structures of Consciousness—Husserl introduces the core problem, which continues to motivate his philosophy of feelings. He sees that feelings are not just affective, but also surprisingly rational. Second, Husserl addresses this enigmatic duality, by pioneering the method of analogizing, which he would employ for the next twenty years. In sum, I show that the 1896 manuscript introduces the problems and methods, in the absence of which Husserl’s later phenomenology of feelings appears inconceivable.
10.5840/philtoday2024126519.title: The Dawn of the Phenomenology of Feelings

10.5840/philtoday202444523.abstract: In Graham Harman’s Object-Oriented Ontology (OOO), an apparent tension arises between his pursuit of a self-proclaimed “new theory of everything,” or general ontology, and his assertion that any ontology must be able to account for distinctions among various regions of being. This paper delves into this tension between universality and specificity, particularly concerning the question of animal ontology, and examines the potential for constructing an object-oriented animal ontology. By juxtaposing Harman’s perspectives with those of Matthew Calarco and other scholars, I aim to demonstrate the feasibility of developing an animal ontology using the framework of OOO.
10.5840/philtoday202444523.title: Object-Oriented Animals: Towards a Theory of Animality in OOO

10.5840/philtoday202449528.abstract: This paper offers a neo-Aristotelian approach to PCSR aimed at enabling us to more systematically ascertain which sorts of corporate political activities, if any, might be politically acceptable. Part 1 sketches Aristotle’s account of the “political.” Aristotelian politics have at least four key dimensions. When we speak of PCSR, we should, from this Aristotelian perspective, evaluate how specific behaviors accord with or undermine these four aspects of political life. Part 2 of the paper explores which forms of activity by corporations qualify as genuinely (and thus acceptably) political within a neo-Aristotelian framework. Part 3 highlights strengths and limitations of this approach to PCSR.
10.5840/philtoday202449528.title: Grounding and Limiting Political Corporate Social Responsibility (PCSR) Using a Neo-Aristotelian Approach

10.5840/philtoday2025228559.abstract: In Difference and Repetition, Deleuze evokes dramatization when he suggests that intensities must dramatize the Ideas to condition their actualization. This allusion to an artistic category, in the midst of his metaphysical inquiry, has remained obscure. It is not clear, despite its cruciality, why he employs dramatization to explain any actualization and not solely artistic actualization. This essay elucidates this ambiguity, while foregrounding a zone of torsional continuity, wherein intensity encounters the Idea and expresses it through dramatization. This process is at play in the actualization of the organic field, social field, and aesthetic field, where an intensive larval subject—embryo, free individual, artist—encounters the biological, social, or artistic Idea. While unraveling the structure of artistic experience, it is shown how dramatization is indispensable to actualize every Idea. Finally, through Tarkovsky and Blanchot, the notion of poeticization is formulated that, while complementing dramatization, unveils some of its tacit nuances.
10.5840/philtoday2025228559.title: Dramatization and Poeticization: Deleuze and the Poeticity of Metaphysics

10.5840/philtoday20267011.abstract: This essay introduces the contents of a special issue of Philosophy Today on climate change. It summarizes recent climate science and a UN proclamation that we have entered a new era of climate change. It outlines the issue’s theme—the planetary—and describes the conditions of a planetary age. It then provides a précis of the thirty-one essays, translations, interviews, book reviews, and communiqués in the special issue. It concludes with a call to assemble as friends of all the living.
10.5840/philtoday20267011.title: Philosophy in a Planetary Age: A Special Issue of Philosophy Today on Climate Change

10.5840/philtoday202670110.abstract: Climate change provokes moral, ethical and political (and aesthetic) reactions that have to do with guilt and shame. The upscaling of guilt and shame to Earth magnitude brings huge risks and huge creative opportunities. It’s best to realize that guilt and shame are what make us human, indeed what make us conscious beings as such. There is no way to rid ourselves of this “structural guilt.” Knowing this brings much relief and inspires us to engage in a perpetual struggle against automated, default ways of behaving aggressively, interpersonally, and socially.
10.5840/philtoday202670110.title: Exposed: How to Enjoy Living Ugly Truths on a Changing Planet

10.5840/philtoday202670111.abstract: We are standing on the cusp of a new era. The time when we are on the threshold can be characterized as the Anthropocene. However, the important background of the Anthropocene can be traced back to the emergence of modern civilization. Furthermore, as we will see, Francis Bacon’s view of human life against this background should be considered to bring about our era as the Anthropocene epoch, albeit among other causes. Against the strong stream of this epoch, the present paper insists that you are not necessarily forced to obey the formidable tendency of technological civilization and the planet Earth’s uncertain wandering in the future. Ultimately, whether you can be free from them and rule yourself is up to you.
10.5840/philtoday202670111.title: "Enforc’d Obedience of Planetary Influence"?

10.5840/philtoday202670112.title: Remembering the Life of the Earth: From Gregory Bateson to Plato

10.5840/philtoday202670113.title: Politics of Nature: Signposts from the Anthropocene

10.5840/philtoday202670114.abstract: This is the transcript of a written exchange that Robin Celikates and Matthias Fritsch carried out between November 2024 and March 2025. We focus the conversation on civil disobedience in response to climate change and in the context of massive global and intergenerational injustices. We discuss climate disobedience as a paradigm case of the politicizing and democratizing force that civil disobedience can be in response to wide-spread entrenched and often invisibilized forms of domination and depoliticization. Drawing on critical rather than ideal theory, we pay special attention to the role disobedience plays in accounts of radical democracy and in relation to ecological destabilization.
10.5840/philtoday202670114.title: Discussing Climate Disobedience in the Capitalocene

10.5840/philtoday202670115.title: Trilogue for Philosophy Today: On Environmental Philosophy’s Collaborative Teamwork in a Planetary Age

10.5840/philtoday20267013.abstract: This essay originally appeared in French as the Introduction to Joëlle Zask’s Quand la forêt brûle. Penser la nouvelle catastrophe écologique (Premier Parallèle, 2019). The book received France Culture’s 2020 Petrarch Essay Prize, which is awarded each year to a work that sheds light on contemporary democratic issues. When the Forest Burns examines the recent phenomenon of very large wildfires or megafires and human beings’ relationship to them. Due to climate change, the size of these wildfires are on a different scale and unprecedented, they are no longer able to be controlled or contained by human beings, and they are becoming more common and increasing in size. Zask, a specialist in democratic theory, John Dewey, and aesthetics, has recently written on ecology and environmental philosophy. Zask teaches in the Philosophy Department at the University of Aix-Marseille and is a member of the Institut Universitaire de France.
10.5840/philtoday20267013.title: Introduction to When the Forest Burns: Thinking the New Ecological Catastrophe

10.5840/philtoday20267014.abstract: A reflection from pan-European climate justice collective WeSmellGas written in summer 2025. We argue that the conversation around climate change has been hijacked by fundamentally technocratic conversations about carbon emissions, peddled by liberal elites and fossil fuel PR teams alike. European climate movements have too often subsumed such narratives. This has nudged liberal, western states towards a highly extractive and colonial “green” transition with little accountability from the social movements of the European left. We urge those engaged with climate resistance to look to the root of the crisis; an extractive, imperialist energy model. We urge the climate struggle in the so-called west, to stand shoulder to shoulder with our siblings on the frontlines of imperialist violence, whether they are our neighbours facing fuel poverty or our siblings resisting ongoing Israel/US genocide of Palestinians in Gaza.
10.5840/philtoday20267014.title: Summer 2025 Statement

10.5840/philtoday20267015.title: From “Banana [    ]: A History of the Americas”

10.5840/philtoday20267016.abstract: From 2020 to 2024, the Centre Pompidou held a series of gatherings called Planetarium, which brought together artists and researchers to explore our planetary condition. Here curator Charlène Dinhut and curator and philosopher Mathieu Potte-Bonneville reflect on the series. They describe the creative and intellectual contributions to the series; historical events throughout the series from climate impacts to major protests to the COVID-19 pandemic; and the role of Bruno Latour.
10.5840/philtoday20267016.title: Planetarium: An Atlas for the World to Come

10.5840/philtoday20267017.title: Reflection, Ebb of a Spring Tide

10.5840/philtoday20267018.abstract: Calls to environmental action invite us to love each other and ourselves enough to do something. That we might breathe deeply without filling one lung with fires and the other with factories. And build homes not permanently under threat of being wind-whipped apart, or splintered by trees, or logged with water for weeks. Such calls enjoin us, too, to love the fauna and flora—typically the most charismatic—enough to guard their habitats and their passage. But few would think to build a movement on the love of rock. Drawing on Indigenous, feminist, queer, and disability literatures, however, this essay makes precisely that fragile proposal.
10.5840/philtoday20267018.title: For the Love of Rock

10.5840/philtoday20267019.title: Even in Arcadia, There We Are

10.5840/philtoday2026710614.abstract: This paper is an affirmation of the legacy of the work of Gianni Vattimo. It attempts to bring to light the radicality of Vattimo’s thought from within the postmodern and nihilistic situation that his work confronted. This is the situation whereby interpretations are deemed to haunt each attempt to determine truth, where every figure of truth appears to be weakened in its own decline and thrown into a constant refutation which doubles back upon its own claim to (the) truth (of untruth). From this situation—and its philosophical problematics—this paper affirms Vattimo’s response to such a decline by overviewing a general picture of the core of his ontology of (the history of) Being. In excavating its core, this paper then points to an alternative approach to the decline of truth following Vattimo’s gift of weakening Being.
10.5840/philtoday2026710614.title: Vattimo’s Gift: Letting Weakness Be

10.5840/philtoday2026710615.abstract: This essay rethinks the relationship between Gianni Vattimo and Hans-Georg Gadamer by situating hermeneutics “after history.” Against Gadamer’s grounding of understanding in the continuity of tradition, I read Vattimo’s ontology of actuality as a displacement of history’s authority, refiguring it as a material for interpretation rather than a metaphysical foundation. I frame this displacement through the tension between legacy and archive, where the material remainder of historical meaning is activated by interpretation in the present. In this sense, Vattimo’s hermeneutics begins not with a fidelity to tradition, but by attending to its disruption, disorientation, and distortion. His ontology of actuality affirms being as emerging through situated, interpretive acts of retrieval that open meaning to risk and contingency. Thus, I suggest a hermeneutics after history, where interpretation displaces tradition through a reorientation towards actuality.
10.5840/philtoday2026710615.title: Hermeneutics After History: Vattimo, Gadamer, and the Ontology of Actuality

10.5840/philtoday2026720616.abstract: All of Jacob Taubes’s reflections on the connection between theology and politics presuppose his engagement with Carl Schmitt’s thought. This text aims to reconstruct the relationship between these thinkers, considering the materials that Taubes collected in the 1987 Berlin publication and their correspondence. The two versions—the indirect account as recounted by Taubes and the direct account furnished by the letters—offer the most relevant insights into the key concepts of political theology and critical theory as they emerge in the work of the two thinkers. They also help us to reconstruct the essential theoretical lines of the troubled relationship between the Jewish Jacob Taubes and the Catholic and Nazi Carl Schmitt.
10.5840/philtoday2026720616.title: Theology and Political Theory Between Taubes and Schmitt

10.5840/philtoday2026722617.abstract: Recent years have seen the emergence, in some quarters, of a debate concerning the current state of critique and its continued viability. Initiated by Bruno Latour in a 2004 paper, the discussion gained impetus with Rita Felski’s 2015 volume The Limits of Critique. The changing political landscape has also contributed to the sense that critique, and critical practice more generally, is undergoing something of a crisis. This paper takes up several ideas that lie in the background of the discussion (although touched upon in Felski’s treatment) that can also be seen to be at issue in older debates between hermeneutics and critical theory, as well as in the tension between philosophical and social-theoretic, literary, and cultural approaches. A fundamental question is that which Felski raises concerning the limits of critique, but here understood as directed, not only at where critique may come to an end, but also where it begins.
10.5840/philtoday2026722617.title: Critique and Its Limits

10.5840/philtoday2026722618.abstract: Taking Amber Guyger’s 2019 trial for the murder of Botham Jean as a point of departure, this article uses the work of Vladimir Jankélévitch and Saidiya Hartman to consider the structural relationship between anti-Blackness and forgiveness, and more specifically the way forgiveness functions to maintain and reinscribe anti-Blackness and the afterlives of slavery. I argue that, whereas Jankélévitch and others center the forgiving subject’s agency in their accounts, the structure of anti-Blackness displaces the Black subject and complicates any conception of their agency, thereby rendering Black forgiveness into a gift which has always already been taken for granted by whiteness, but which the Black subject must nevertheless freely give and bear.
10.5840/philtoday2026722618.title: Gratuity Included: Anti-Blackness and the Gift of Forgiveness

10.5840/philtoday2026723619.abstract: Ensuring that intelligent machines align with human values and ethical principles is a critical challenge of our time. This paper proposes a novel approach to improve rule-based ethical AI systems. We introduce three principles derived from Martin Heidegger’s philosophy: Autotelism, Sociality, and Finitude, as context-sensitive ethical guidelines. These principles ensure that AI prioritizes its proper functioning while recognizing its embeddedness in social and finite contexts. Unlike rigid rule-based systems, which struggle to apply rules in complex and novel situations, our principle-based approach enables adaptive decision-making through a method we term principle-guided situational understanding. By integrating these principles, we provide a philosophical foundation that complements technical efforts in AI alignment, fostering machines that are both intelligent and ethically attuned to the human lifeworld.
10.5840/philtoday2026723619.title: Heideggerian AI Ethics: Principles for AI Alignment

10.5840/philtoday2026723620.abstract: This paper analyzes Heidegger’s understanding of writing as it plays out within the Four Booklets (in GA 99). By bringing certain passages into conversation with Jacques Derrida’s critique of Heidegger’s alleged logocentrism, I argue that GA 99 demonstrates a commitment on Heidegger’s part to an originary inscription that precedes and makes possible spoken discourse. As a consequence, GA 99 shows Heidegger attempting to think radical difference (i.e., dissemination) in a manner much closer to Derrida than scholars have typically thought.
10.5840/philtoday2026723620.title: (Re)Writing the World: Heidegger and the Inscription

10.5840/philtoday2026723621.abstract: This essay considers Peter Sloterdijk’s reading of deconstruction as a “transport science” to critique a globalized “science” of space. In arguing that Derrida’s philosophy can be interpreted “as a method of defending intelligence against the consequences of one-sidedness,” Sloterdijk takes seriously the textual movement of deconstructive thought, redirecting attention back to space and spacing. Sloterdijk’s emphasis on thinking space in post-globalization philosophy can be extended by considering Derrida’s attention to the spatial relation between science and writing—and how it determines our understanding of “life.” This argument is built out of Sloterdijk’s short book on Derrida to broader themes in his work—most notably, his reflections on globalization and its space-reducing effects. Reading these through Derrida’s critique of a monumentalist metaphysics that circles science around the fixed insides of memory, this essay argues that we should instead consider space as writing, the ongoing production of meanings that transports thinking outside.
10.5840/philtoday2026723621.title: Transport Science: Placing Deconstruction, Outside the Monument-World

10.5840/philtoday2026724622.abstract: This paper focuses on the work of Alphonso Lingis’s critique of thanatocentric thinking, namely the pervasive notion that a proper understanding of life must be framed in relation to death. I argue that Lingis constructs an alternative philosophy of life centered around a threefold system based on the notions of experience, embodiment, and reality. Through an analysis of Lingis’s major works, this article aims to contribute to the evolving field of “Lingisian studies” by highlighting his novel understanding of what it means to be an embodied being in a more-than-human world.
10.5840/philtoday2026724622.title: Against Thanatocentrism: Alphonso Lingis and the Excess of Life

10.5840/philtoday2026724623.abstract: This essay reevaluates Bataille’s perspective on sovereignty, arguing that he introduces a form of sovereign decision characterized by hubris rather than non-sovereignty. Bataille’s state of exaltation, seen as an excessive and uncontrollable ontological predicament, is crucial to his critique of the (non-)sovereign economy. By framing excess as the accursed share, Bataille suggests that the communal treatment of this share allows for a less disastrous form of expenditure. This hubris redirects the state of exaltation, proposing a transformative notion of power beyond utilitarian constraints. Consequently, Bataille challenges conventional notions of sovereignty, advocating for sovereign practice located in the exuberance and inevitability of excess.
10.5840/philtoday2026724623.title: The State of Exaltation and Ontological Hubris

10.5840/philtoday2026724624.abstract: This paper investigates the question of dualism in the work of Georges Bataille, especially through his early period wherein a seeming dualism is most evident. By reading this period alongside his middle and later periods, this paper attempts to show the misrecognition of this early dualism, thus excavating a clear dialectical core to his thought. From this, a conjunction between Bataille and the work of the Ljubljana school and co. comes to light; this paper reconsiders their critiques, especially those of Eric Santner and Slavoj Žižek, given the paper’s conclusions on Bataille’s dialectics.
10.5840/philtoday2026724624.title: The Enemy Within the Enemy: Bataille Reading Bataille

10.5840/philtoday2026724625.abstract: Catherine Malabou’s work on plasticity represents a new encounter with materiality. As a paradigm for conceptualizing the nature of change in non-teleological terms, plasticity endorses a theory of becoming based on matter’s own malleability rather than on unrealized potential. However, notably absent from her work is any direct engagement with Marx’s historical materialism, other than encouraging a “re-molding” and “re-forming” of his thought from plasticity’s perspective. This essay envisions what such re-molding may look like. It maps a strategy by drawing on Malabou’s four aspects of plasticity (giving form, receiving form, explosion, and resistance) to trace the resemblance between plasticity and historical materialism. I suggest that labor, the prototypical Marxist concept, works plastically, building from the inherent malleability of the human rather than from pre-established principles. For the paradigm of plasticity, to re-form Marx, one must start with labor.
10.5840/philtoday2026724625.title: "A Natural History": Plastic Materiality in Marx

10.5840/philtoday202672603.abstract: In both his philosophical and political commitments, Vattimo had consistently made explicit his stance for the weak, the poor, and the excluded. What is the relationship between Weak Thought and poverty? What implications and forms can this relationship take on today? In this paper, I will first emphasize the paradoxical role of weakness, poverty, and reduction in Vattimo. I will then show how the very renunciation of the hegemonic Western arché leads to the anarchic liberation and multiplication of different voices and forms of life. I will finally hint at the subversive and transformative role of these differences, if kept alive in an (inexhaustible) hermeneutical dialogue.
10.5840/philtoday202672603.title: The Adventures of Poverty: From Weak Thought to the Thought of the Weak

10.5840/philtoday202672604.abstract: In this paper, I analyze Vattimo’s advancement of hermeneutics beyond its classical boundaries. Building on his interpretations of Heidegger and Gadamer, Vattimo highlights the emancipatory potential of hermeneutics while critiquing traditional metaphysical frameworks. He advocates for “weak thought” (), a flexible and non-violent approach to truth and interpretation. I argue that Vattimo’s hermeneutics is not merely a theoretical pursuit but a practical and ethical endeavour aimed at reducing metaphysical violence and democratizing knowledge. His approach positions the philosopher as an active participant in societal discourse, insisting that philosophy must engage deeply with contemporary reality, “getting its hands dirty” in the everyday struggles against injustice.
10.5840/philtoday202672604.title: Outside the Ivory Tower: Gianni Vattimo’s Hermeneutics of Engagement

10.5840/philtoday2026729626.abstract: The global environmental crisis necessitates innovative, inclusive strategies, and African indigenous knowledge systems offer valuable insights. This study explores African philosophies such as Ubuntu ecology, eco-bio-communitarianism, and ukama, which emphasize interconnectedness, mutual care, and the intrinsic value of all life. These non-anthropocentric perspectives challenge dominant human-centered approaches, advocating harmony between human well-being and ecological health. Through a critical analysis, the paper identifies shared principles across African environmental models, arguing for an eclectic approach that integrates their strengths. This holistic framework aligns with Africa’s traditional worldview of balance and community, offering practical, culturally resonant solutions to ecological challenges. Incorporating African environmental ethics into global discourses enriches environmental theory with diverse epistemologies, fostering sustainable practices. This study concludes that African philosophies provide a crucial pathway to ecological stewardship, addressing pressing global challenges through a lens of interconnectedness and mutual respect.
10.5840/philtoday2026729626.title: Eclectic African Environmental Ethics: Integrating Indigenous Perspectives for Sustainable Ecological Stewardship

10.5840/philtoday2026729627.abstract: This article explores the theoretical implications immanent in Alfred North Whitehead’s realism, positioning it as a theoretical framework capable of transcending the limitations delineated within Kant’s metaphorical depiction of the island as the land of truth. Kant vividly portrays this island as the locus of truth and reason in a prominent passage in Critique of Pure Reason. By conducting an examination of the foundational principles of process thought, with particular emphasis on the conceptual framework articulated in Whitehead’s seminal treatise, Process and Reality, this study endeavors to reassess the geophilosophical potentials covered by the notion of the island, while simultaneously addressing issues pertaining to subject and superject, object and event, as well as life and value. Through engaging in a critical dialogue with contemporary ontological paradigms, including new realism and Object-Oriented-Ontology (OOO), this article aims to reconceptualize the process philosophy as a cornerstone of contemporary discourse, firmly rooted in the interconnectedness of events that shape the actual world.
10.5840/philtoday2026729627.title: In the Longest Footnote to Western Philosophy: Alfred North Whitehead and Others

10.5840/philtoday2026729628.abstract: This paper examines the philosophical implications of organ transplantation through a comparative analysis of Jean-Luc Nancy’s and Francisco Varela’s post-transplantation writings. Drawing on their first-hand accounts as heart and liver transplant recipients, the paper explores how modern biotechnological interventions fundamentally transform our understanding of selfhood. The analysis reveals that post-transplantation life represents an unprecedented form of existence where traditional notions of self-knowledge and lived experience are radically disrupted. Unlike Michael Polanyi’s assertion that “we know more than we can tell,” transplant recipients find themselves “knowing less than they can tell,” where self-understanding becomes mediated through external medical data. The paper argues that post-transplantation existence creates a unique form of solitude characterized by irreproducible, technologically-mediated life conditions that escape shared experiential and meaning frameworks. This transformation suggests a fundamental shift in conceptualizing the relationship between lived experience and scientific knowledge, where self-knowledge yields to the performativity of technological interventions and medical narratives.
10.5840/philtoday2026729628.title: Knowing Less Than We Can Tell: Jean-Luc Nancy and Francisco Varela on Organ Transplantation and Post-Transplantation Life

10.5840/philtoday2026729629.abstract: Balancing a hermeneutic of trust with a hermeneutic of suspicion, this article develops a phenomenological description of imagination that highlights its alethic ambiguity. Imagination is an act of disclosure, without which the world of fiction and pure possibility cannot be constituted. Imagination is also an act of self-indulgence and narcissism, the source of much concealment and untruth. It is not the one or the other, but both at the same time, essentially ambiguous because of its phenomenological constitution. In this article, I will take some steps towards clarifying this essential ambiguity of the imagination by drawing on the insights of Husserl and Sartre. Beginning with Husserl’s parallel treatment of imagination and perception as intuitive, objectifying acts, I will argue, drawing on insights from Sartre, that there is an important discrepancy between them with respect to the role of desire. While the constitution of perceptual presence is inseparable from a desire for truth, the desire involved in the constitution of imaginary presence has an ambiguous character, both alethic and magical. This duplicity of desire partly accounts for the ambiguity of imagination, which is all the more pronounced the more the imagination demands the full emotional involvement of the imagining subject.
10.5840/philtoday2026729629.title: Truthfulness and Narcissism: Phenomenological Reflections on the Ambiguity of Imagination

10.5840/philtoday202674605.abstract: The renewed interest in communism among continental philosophers such as Jean-Luc Nancy, Alain Badiou, and Slavoj Žižek has catalyzed a range of reinterpretations of Marxist thought in response to the failures of twentieth-century socialism and the persistent crises of global capitalism. Among these, Gianni Vattimo’s concept of hermeneutic communism presents a unique ontological and ethical intervention. Grounded in his philosophical project of “weak thought,” Vattimo envisions communism not as an ideological or revolutionary orthodoxy but as a post-metaphysical practice of interpretation, solidarity, and democratic pluralism. This essay explores Vattimo’s “weak communism” as a response to the metaphysical rigidity and dogmatism that have often characterized both Marxist and liberal traditions. Rather than retreating into relativism, Vattimo’s weakening of metaphysical foundations opens space for a historically grounded, ethically committed politics that resists domination and affirms interpretive responsibility. Drawing on Heidegger’s notion of Geschick (destiny), Vattimo reframes nihilism as a condition of philosophical and political possibility. His work ultimately offers a radical rethinking of communism, one that privileges dialogue over rupture, contingency over certainty, and historical inheritance over doctrinal purity.
10.5840/philtoday202674605.title: The Weak Communism of Gianni Vattimo: A Postmetaphysical Vision of Emancipation

10.5840/philtoday202678606.abstract: This contribution mainly presents an interview with Vattimo at a Dresden conference in 2013. In the conversation, Vattimo reflects on his approach to God as original freedom and as the initiative of his personal freedom. He sees this freedom expressed in biblical language, in particular in images of a weakening God. As a consequence, human beings are given over to themselves by God and are called into self-responsibility. Vattimo thus opens up a view of the secularized present in which not only powerful remnants of religion continue to exist despite secularization, but secularization itself can be understood as a religious, i.e., kenotic process. Vattimo’s perspective discussed in the interview can be a key to perceiving the multidimensional dynamics of secularization in a new light.
10.5840/philtoday202678606.title: God Is the Initiative of Creating Freedom: An Interview with Gianni Vattimo

10.5840/philtoday202678607.abstract: This paper examines Gianni Vattimo’s interpretation of Being as a temporal and interpretative process rather than a static metaphysical foundation. Drawing on Nietzsche and Heidegger, Vattimo frames Being as an event unfolding through history. Central to his project is the notion of Verwindung (convalescence), through which metaphysical structures are weakened and reconfigured rather than decisively overcome. I argue that here we encounter the same tensions that arise in his engagement with secularization: while aiming to overcome metaphysical foundations, his weakening and convalescence also preserves Christianity and Western metaphysics. This ambivalence raises questions about whether weakening leads to liberation or a softened preservation of tradition, inviting further reflection on the challenges of post-metaphysical thought.
10.5840/philtoday202678607.title: Being as Becoming

10.5840/philtoday202678608.abstract: What is the relation between philosophy and the person of the philosopher? And what is the responsibility of the philosopher in the practice of philosophy? Gianni Vattimo is one of the few philosophers directly to address such questions both in general and in relation to his own life and thought. That he does so is itself a reflection of the personal engagement and commitment that characterized much of his thinking. The present essay is an attempt to explore a little of what is at issue here, especially as it relates to hermeneutics, as well as to express something of my own gratitude for having been lucky enough to have known Gianni, and the affection and respect I have for him.
10.5840/philtoday202678608.title: To Speak the Truth: Gianni Vattimo and the Responsibility of the Philosopher

10.5840/philtoday202679609.abstract: Not Being God: A Collaborative Autobiography, which Gianni Vattimo published in 2006 with the collaboration of Piergiorgio Paterlini, is a book-length interview that opens the way to a new way of understanding philosophical autobiography. Through a theoretical recognition of the concept of philosophical autobiography, starting with Montaigne and continuing to the present, this essay highlights how the points of Gianni Vattimo’s philosophical thought constitute a fil rouge that crosses an entire existence lived as a theoretical project in action. After an introductory section examining Vattimo’s models in the tradition of philosophical autobiography, this essay seeks to understand how his work represented a turning point and a reference model for the autobiographical writings of contemporary philosophers.
10.5840/philtoday202679609.title: Autobiographical Writing and the Reconfigurations of Being a Philosopher

10.5840/philtoday202679610.abstract: This article navigates Vattimo’s theorizations for a borderless aesthetics. A close examination of two manuscripts where Vattimo develops the critical terms of oscillation and heterotopia will lead to the disclosure of the weakening of aesthetics. Such a process is essential for elaborating an interpretive framework able to provide the tools to rethink the intersection of political and artistic practices in contemporary societies, rife with crises and states of emergency. The weakening of aesthetics concurs with the weakening of truth, no longer identifiable with a static idea of veritas, but, instead, encapsulated in the dynamic frame of alētheia. This radical hermeneutic restructuring attempts to reflect on the broader implications of a borderless aesthetics based on oscillation and oriented heterotopically, perpetually dialoguing with the ecological and political challenges of the present.
10.5840/philtoday202679610.title: Borderless Aesthetics: Art, Oscillation, and Heterotopia in Vattimo’s Thought

10.5840/philtoday202679611.abstract: At the end of the 1980s the Italian philosopher Gianni Vattimo published two essays in exhibition catalogues issued in conjunction with museum shows of the work of maverick contemporary American artist James Lee Byars. Vattimo’s post-modern philosophy of il pensiero debole found common ground with the idiosyncratic conceptual and performance art practiced by Byars. In particular, the theses on the death or decline of art proposed in Vattimo’s 1985 La fine della modernità (The End of Modernity, 1988) were embraced by the philosophically-minded Byars, especially as crystallized in the notion of Verwindung—namely, the disenchantment of the Western tradition through a distortion that also constitutes a convalescence from its metaphysical violence—that the Italian philosopher set at the center of his project of “weak thinking.” The present essay explores this intercontinental encounter between philosopher and artist as they individually pursue the articulation and representation of the “perfect thought” of post-modernity.
10.5840/philtoday202679611.title: Perfect Thoughts and il pensiero debole

10.5840/philtoday202679612.abstract: Gianni Vattimo wrote prolifically about art, scattering insightful interpretations of literature, poetry, and photography across many of his books and essays. The one artform he did not seem much interested in, though, was cinema. In only a handful of texts did Vattimo comment on the movies. But these musings—about Charlie Chaplin’s Modern Times (1936), say, or the Coen Brothers’ A Serious Man (2009)—signal an appreciation of film’s philosophical potential that remains unexplored in the secondary literature devoted to Vattimo’s life and legacy. After surveying some of his brief remarks about film art, including his analysis—in The Transparent Society—of Walter Benjamin’s famous essay “The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction,” the following outlines an approach to motion picture interpretation that might adequately reflect Vattimo’s hermeneutical, kenotic, and ontological understanding of aesthetics, emphasizing the formative, ongoing interaction of artists, audiences, and the movies.
10.5840/philtoday202679612.title: Vattimo at the Movies

10.5840/philtoday202679613.abstract: This article examines Gianni Vattimo’s concept of weak thought, outlining its key elements and discussing its limitations in a cross-cultural context. While Vattimo’s weak thought dismantles absolute principles and embraces ethical plurality, it remains largely confined to the Western philosophical tradition. For Vattimo, the history of Being is a process of weakening that is inseparable from its Western roots. Although this framework critiques metaphysical rigidity and promotes pluralism, its Eurocentric focus risks perpetuating the exclusions it seeks to address, limiting meaningful dialogue with other philosophical traditions. I conclude that a development of weak thought should not be confined within the Western philosophical canon; rather, it should engage with other philosophical traditions that can resonate with it. As an example, I propose to relate weak thought to the Chinese concept of wuwei 無為 as articulated in the Daodejing 道德經. Such cross-cultural resonance could redefine weakening as a decolonial praxis, opening pathways for philosophy to engage equitably with diverse traditions while actively dismantling entrenched structures of dominance.
10.5840/philtoday202679613.title: Weakening Boundaries: Gianni Vattimo’s Weak Thought Beyond Eurocentrism
